Model Output:
The studio smells of pine cleaner and the sharp, metallic sweat of bodies that have been here since dawn. I am at the southwest corner, my left shoulder almost touching the wooden barre on the west wall. The mirror is north—a long, silver wall that shows me every flaw with merciless clarity. Master Hwang stands south-center, facing north, his black suit a vertical blade against the white. Three other trainees hold their marks in a perfect grid: one at northeast, one at southeast, one at northwest. I am the fourth point of the square, but I feel like a smudge. He opens his hand fan—bamboo ribs clicking like teeth—then snaps it shut. The sound is a gunshot. “Begin,” he says. I step to center. My feet land in second position, shoulder-width apart, facing north. The taped cross on the floor is my only anchor. Count one: I snap my head to the right—east—sharp, mechanical. The motion is clean, but my hair, untamed and not pulled into the sleek ponytails of the others, moves with a delay, a ghost of my old self. Count two: Right shoulder pops back, facing south. I feel my collarbone want to roll into a wave, a liquid motion from years of cipher battles in the alleyways of Guro-dong, where I learned to bend time with my body. I cut it. I am not here to groove. Count three: Both arms extend to a high V, forty-five degrees from vertical, fingers spread but frozen. Left arm mirrors right. Count four: Hold. The mirror shows me: my elbows are at forty-three degrees, not forty-five. I adjust. The other trainees do not adjust. They are already architecture. Master Hwang snaps his fan shut. “Again,” he says. I restart at center. The choreography demands militaristic precision—every angle a command, every hit a weapon. I am a street dancer from the concrete blocks of Cheongnyang; my body knows flow, bounce, improvisation. This is the opposite. This is a formation drill, and I am out of formation. Count five: Pivot one-eighty degrees clockwise on the ball of my right foot. My left foot lands facing south—away from the mirror, toward Master Hwang. I am at center, facing south. Count six: I step back with my left foot to downstage center—closer to him, south of the taped cross. My right foot joins. I am at DC, facing south, feet together. Count seven: I hit the pose. Right arm extends straight out at shoulder height, pointing west—toward center. Left hand strikes my hip. My knees bend to exactly ninety degrees—deep, mechanical, unyielding. Count eight: Hold. My thighs burn. In the streets, I would bounce, find the groove, let my knees be loose, responsive to the beat. Here, they are locks. Count nine: Pop knees up—extend. Lock elbows at forty-five degrees. Right elbow points up and out (northeast), left elbow points down and out (southwest). I am a broken robot. Count ten: Head snaps to face north, toward the mirror. Count eleven: Hold. Count twelve: I travel. From DC, I step left with my left foot to center. Then right foot to upstage left—the northwest corner, near the mirror’s edge. I am at UL, facing north. Count thirteen: Hold at UL. Right leg extends back (south), left leg bent at ninety degrees. Right arm points down at forty-five degrees toward the floor. My body is angled forty-five degrees to the mirror. I feel the cold of the wall against my shoulder. Master Hwang snaps his fan. “Hold,” he says. I hold. The other trainees are already at their next marks, synchronized with a precision that makes my breath feel loud. Count fourteen: I step back with my right foot to center. Left foot joins. I am at C. Count fifteen: Sharp turn ninety degrees counter-clockwise on the ball of my left foot. I now face west—toward the barre. Count sixteen: Hit pose. Right arm horizontal to west. Left arm vertical, pointing up. Elbows locked. Count seventeen to twenty: Locking sequence. Head snaps to north. Shoulder isolates to right—sharp, not rolled. Right arm hits high V. Hold. My shoulder wants to roll into a wave, that liquid street motion I used to win battles, but I hit it sharp, a point of impact. Count twenty-one: I travel again. From C, I step right with my right foot to downstage right—the southeast corner. Left foot joins. I am at DR. Count twenty-two: Sharp turn to face north. Count twenty-three: Hold at DR. Feet in first position, together. Arms at sharp ninety-degree angles—right arm horizontal to east, left arm vertical up. Count twenty-four: I step back with left foot to center. Right foot joins. I am at C, facing north. The “chorus point” approaches—the signature move of the song, the moment where every trainee hits the same angle at the same beat. Count twenty-five: I step to my final mark—downstage left, the southwest corner near the barre. Feet together. Count twenty-six: Turn to face north. Count twenty-seven: I begin the final hit. The choreography demands a static freeze: arms snap to sharp ninety-degree angles, elbows pointing out like a bird’s wings broken at the joint, body frozen at forty-five degrees to the mirror, knees locked, spine straight, head tilted down at exactly forty-five degrees. But my muscle memory betrays me. I feel it in my ankles—the bounce I used to keep time in the cipher. It travels up: knees want to be loose, hips want to sway, spine wants to curve into a wave, that fluid “body roll” that is the language of my neighborhood. My left hand flicks—not to the sharp angle, but to a loose, expressive gesture, a street “wave” that leaks out like a secret. I have a split second. The choice is physical, visceral. I can lock my joints and become the machine—hit the point, win the scholarship, survive. Or I can let the wave take over, insert my authentic voice into the formation, and fail. I feel the class anxiety like a cold hand on my throat. The others have parents who are producers, bodies already remade into instruments of synchronization. I am a scholarship kid from the alleyways, my shoes scuffed, my jacket from a thrift store. If I conform, I lose my voice. If I rebel, I lose the only ladder I have. I make the choice. I snap my elbows to the sharp angle. I freeze. I kill the wave. But as I hold the pose—feet at the southwest corner, facing north, arms in the precise “V” of the choreography—I feel my authentic movement voice leaving me, like breath leaving a body. I have chosen survival over soul. Master Hwang snaps his fan shut. “Good,” he says. His voice is tight, almost disappointed. “You have potential. I see it in your isolations. But your attitude—this is not a cipher. You are not in a battle. You are in a formation.” He looks at me—at my frozen body, at the microscopic flick of my left hand that was almost, almost a wave, at the way I am holding the pose but feeling the absence inside it. “I will remake you,” he says. “Or you will break.” I stand at the southwest corner, facing north, my body a machine now. The mirror shows me: I am precise. I am correct. I am lost. The fan is open again, ready for the next drill. I take a breath. The rhythm of the studio is not the rhythm of my streets. But I have survived this cycle. Whether I can survive the next—whether I will let them break the wave out of me, or whether I will find a way to keep it hidden inside the lock—is the question that stays in my joints, vibrating like a frequency I can no longer hear. I hold the pose. I do not move. I wait for the next snap.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates exceptional technical execution in fulfilling the prompt's demanding requirements. The writer maintains meticulous spatial tracking throughout, with precise choreographic notation that allows readers to visualize every movement, position, and transition in the studio space. The compass directions, body angles, and stage positions create a vivid kinetic map that never loses coherence. The contrast between street dance fluidity and K-pop precision is expertly rendered through both physical description and internal conflict. The protagonist's muscle memory betraying them with street moves ("the bounce," "the wave") while trying to execute mechanical precision creates genuine tension. The technical dance terminology feels authentic and serves the narrative rather than showing off. The first-person voice is consistent and compelling, capturing the protagonist's cultural displacement, class anxiety, and artistic identity crisis. The internal monologue reveals layers of conflict without becoming overwrought. The character's decision to conform feels earned given the established stakes and pressures. The prose is generally elegant, with strong sensory details (pine cleaner smell, metallic sweat, fan snapping like gunshots) that ground the reader in the space. The writing maintains clarity while building emotional intensity through the choreographed sequence. However, some passages veer toward purple prose, particularly in metaphorical descriptions ("vertical blade against the white," "I am a broken robot"). While evocative, these occasionally feel forced. The ending, while thematically appropriate, relies somewhat heavily on explicit statement of the protagonist's loss rather than letting it emerge purely through action. The piece succeeds in creating genuine emotional engagement through the protagonist's impossible choice between authenticity and survival. The cultural and class tensions feel real and specific rather than generic. The technical precision demanded by the prompt is met without sacrificing narrative momentum or emotional truth. + Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 86.8
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The chamber was not a room but a held breath. Obsidian walls breathed slowly, and somewhere a clock ticked in a language that had not yet been invented. Dream sat upon his bench—not quite seated, not quite standing—wearing the expression of a man asked to referee a quarrel between two ants over a crumb of bread. His eyes were stars that had forgotten to shine. The bailiff rose, if “rose” was the word for a shadow unfolding itself into a shape too large for dignity. He spoke with a voice like thunder wrapped in velvet. “All rise—no, remain seated, posture is a lie—this Court of the Dreaming is now in session! Case: Territorial Dream Dispute, The Dreamscape of Max, juvenile human, contested. For the plaintiff, First Love—FRIST LOVEE, the Rosy-Cheeked Fabricator of Formative Romance! For the defense, Mora—MO-RAH, the Slavic Nightmare, also called MORAY, the Chest-Sitter and Breath-Feeder! The bailiff will now mispronounce all further names for the record!” Dream sighed, a sound like dry leaves in a cathedral. “Proceed. Briefly. I have a nightmare about a lost library that requires my attention, and I find recurring dreams to be a particular nuisance. They clutter the docket.” First Love shivered into visibility. He was rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful, and wore a suit of pastel colors that seemed to apologize for existing. “I… I created the dream,” First Love said, voice like a flute in a distant meadow. “Max, the schoolboy. He lies in a field of wildflowers. His crush joins him. There is muddled emotion. There is an almost-kiss. There is pleasant confusion. It is formative.” Mora materialized. She was heavy, dark, and possessed the kind of presence that made the air feel pressed from above. She sat, naturally, upon an invisible chest, though no sleeper was present to feel it. “I invaded it,” Mora said, with the cheerful practicality of a landlord discussing renovations. “The girl mounts him playfully. She morphs into a terrifying yet confusingly attractive vision. She sits on his chest. She feeds on his breath. It is efficient.” First Love blushed. “But the almost-kiss! The confusion of emotions! She was meant to feel… hopeful!” “Hope is a luxury,” Mora said. “A girl’s gotta eat too, you know?” Dream leaned forward. “You are aware this is a romantic construct?” “I am aware that breath is a resource,” Mora said. “He breathes. I eat. The wildflowers are decorative.” The bailiff boomed: “Objection! The witness—MORA—has just admitted to consuming a juvenile human’s respiration! The court reporter—who is also a spider—will note this!” “Overruled,” Dream said, though he looked only mildly interested. “Continue.” First Love spoke of the invasion. How the girl, in her playful mounting, had become terrifying yet still confusingly attractive. How Mora’s presence had turned the almost-kiss into a suffocation. How Max woke not with longing but with paralysis, his heart hammering against a weight that smelled of old earth and something almost like perfume. “I merely adjusted the architecture,” Mora said. “The dream is bigger now. It serves a practical purpose.” Dream glanced at the gallery, where shadows shifted like uncomfortable guests. “You claim ownership?” “I claim possession,” Mora corrected. “I sit upon it. I feed from it. The breath is mine.” First Love wrung his hands. “But the confusion! It was meant to be pleasant! Now it is terror with a twist of romance?” “Exactly,” Mora said. “I am confusingly attractive. It is a feature, not a bug.” Dream felt a strange, mischievous itch in the place where his heart might have been, if he had permitted himself one. He considered the evidence: the wildflowers, the almost-kiss, the breath, the paralysis. It was absurd. It was perfect. “First Love,” Dream said softly, “you are a craftsman of formative experiences. Mora, you are a parasite of the sleeping. You have both altered Max. But ownership of a dreamscape is not merely about who sits upon it. It is about who sustains it.” He stood. The chamber seemed to hold its breath. “The Court finds that Mora has established adverse possession through continuous occupation and consumption. The dreamscape of Max is hereby awarded to Mora. She may sit upon his chest and feed upon his breath as she wishes.” First Love wilted. “But,” Dream continued, “because First Love retains the emotional copyright to the wildflowers and the almost-kiss sequence, Mora is hereby required to maintain them. The breath she feeds upon must remain sweet with longing. The girl must continue to mount him playfully before the transformation, because the transition is what produces the confusion he finds… delightful.” Mora’s eyes narrowed. “You are binding me to the romance.” “I am binding you to the architecture,” Dream said. “If you destroy the wildflowers, you forfeit the territory. If you prevent the almost-kiss, the breath turns sour, and you will find yourself starving in a field of thorns.” Dream smiled—not with warmth, but with the particular mischief of a god who has arranged an elegant trap. “Furthermore,” Dream said, “because this dream is now a shared ecology—Mora feeding, First Love crafting—the confusion of emotions will remain. Max will wake each morning with a peculiar cocktail of dread and affection. He will be slightly more cautious and slightly more hopeful. And because I oversee the Dreaming, I have decided that this particular blend will serve as a template. Mora, wherever you go next, you will find that the breath of your next victim smells of wildflowers. You will always carry this dream with you.” The bailiff boomed: “The Court has ruled! The dreamscape belongs to Mora, but she is a tenant of her own appetite! All witnesses are hereby mispronounced for eternity!” Mora stood, heavy and triumphant, but suddenly burdened. “A girl’s gotta eat,” she said, though her voice had lost some of its certainty. “Indeed,” Dream said, returning to his bench. “And now she must do so in a field of flowers, with a girl who almost kisses her. It is a punishment, Mora. You have been outmaneuvered by romance.” First Love blushed, faintly relieved. The bailiff mispronounced the final names with thunderous finality: “Mora—MO-RAH, the Bound Chest-Sitter! First Love—FRIST LOVEE, the Eternal Bait! Court is adjourned!” Dream did not look up. “Next case. And bailiff—get the spider to file this under ‘ironic.’” The chamber exhaled. The dream continued, wildflowers intact, the almost-kiss preserved, the breath feeding a nightmare that was now, permanently and legally, in love with its own terror.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt's requirements, successfully creating a dark fantasy courtroom scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream. The author captures Dream's characteristic voice and demeanor effectively, portraying his irritation at adjudicating such matters while maintaining his otherworldly authority. The characterizations are well-executed and nuanced. First Love is appropriately bashful and romantic, Mora is pragmatically predatory with her "a girl's gotta eat" defense, and Dream maintains his typical inscrutability while revealing subtle mischief. The bailiff serves as effective comic relief with his mispronunciation gimmick. The prose style is elegant and restrained, avoiding purple prose while maintaining atmospheric descriptions. Lines like "The chamber was not a room but a held breath" and "His eyes were stars that had forgotten to shine" establish the dreamlike setting without overindulgence. The dialogue feels authentic to each character and advances both plot and comedy effectively. The comedic elements work well through the absurdity of the situation - a nightmare spirit arguing property rights over a teenage boy's romantic dream. The humor remains appropriately dark and understated as requested, emerging from character interactions rather than forced jokes. The resolution is particularly clever, with Dream's mischievous judgment that binds Mora to maintain the romantic elements while granting her possession. This creates an ironic punishment that serves the story's themes while providing satisfying closure. The ending avoids unearned positivity - it's more of a darkly comic compromise than a happy resolution. The piece maintains coherent internal logic throughout and flows naturally from setup through resolution. The courtroom procedural elements blend seamlessly with the fantastical setting. The writing demonstrates sophistication in balancing multiple tones and requirements without becoming overwrought or meandering. Minor weaknesses include some moments where the whimsical elements (like the spider court reporter) feel slightly forced, and the bailiff's repeated mispronunciation gag, while amusing, borders on becoming tiresome. However, these are minor issues in an otherwise well-crafted piece that successfully fulfills a complex set of requirements. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 54.8
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Blood Moon** The wolves howl at irregular intervals, a ragged chorus that stitches across the darkened valley of medieval Europe. Their cries do not synchronize; they come in broken clusters, as if each beast is answering a different, private grief. The air tastes of iron and old snow. Alucard stands in the center of a ruined chapel’s courtyard, his red coat a wound against the gray stone, his wide-brimmed hat casting a shadow that swallows his face. Orange sunglasses hide his eyes—eyes that have watched centuries burn—but they do not hide the smile that curves beneath them. He holds one of his massive handguns, the barrel thick as a man’s arm, loaded with silver bullets that glint like teeth in the moonlight. He is waiting. He always waits for something worthy. She arrives without sound, though the wolves fall silent as she steps from the treeline. Yennefer of Vengerberg moves with the deliberate grace of a woman who has paid dearly for every inch of her posture, her congenital hunchback magically erased, her appearance sculpted into something that could turn heads at court or on a battlefield. She smells of lilac and gooseberries, a scent so precise, so deliberately cultivated, that it seems almost aggressive against the rot of the woods. Her violet eyes catch the moon, and she does not flinch when she sees him. A monster. She thinks it immediately, and the word is not just descriptive but visceral. He is a vampire—ancient, vast, a thing that should not exist in the light of reason. She is repulsed by the monstrosity of him, by the way his coat seems to drink the darkness, by the casual cruelty in his posture, by the orange lenses that make him look like a predator wearing a mask. And yet, fascination coils in her chest, cold and sharp. She has faced dragons, Nilfgaardian generals, and the Council’s politics; she has never faced something that wants to toy with her before killing her. “You smell like flowers,” Alucard says. His voice is smooth, arrogant, a predator’s purr. He does not lower the gun. “How quaint. I was expecting a witch with more sense than to wander into a graveyard without a circle.” “The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame,” he continues, and the quote hangs in the air like a challenge. “But I don’t think I’ll be tamed tonight, witch. Not by you.” Yennefer’s lips twitch—not a smile, but something close to contempt. “I’m not sweet and I’m not a maiden in distress in need of saving,” she says, her voice sharp enough to cut glass. She raises her hands, and the air between them shimmers with violet light. “You think your silver and your red coat make you terrifying? You’re just another predator who thinks he’s special.” She casts. Not a simple fireball—she is too clever for that. She weaves a binding of elemental force, a cage of ice and flame that should hold a lesser creature. Alucard does not flinch. He lets the magic strike him, and his body ripples, shape-shifting in an instant, his form blurring like smoke. The cage passes through empty air where he stood, and he is behind her, or beside her, or already moving. “You’re quick,” he admits, and there is genuine surprise in his tone, which is worse than mockery. He fires the handgun—not at her, but at the ground near her feet, and the silver bullet explodes in a shower of sparks that burn the earth black. “But quick isn’t enough. You need to be worthy.” She dodges, her magic instinctive, her body moving with the fluidity of someone who has reshaped her own bones, who has hidden her true form behind glamour and will. She turns, and for a moment their eyes meet—his hidden behind orange lenses, hers blazing violet—and she feels the pull of his monstrous nature, the ancient hunger that is not merely physical but existential. She wants to destroy him. She wants to understand him. She wants, with a desperation she refuses to acknowledge, to see if he can be broken, because if he can, perhaps she can be fixed too. The wolves howl again, irregular and distant, as if they are calling to something they do not understand. Alucard circles her, the red coat swirling, the hat tilted at a mocking angle. He is playing with her, and she knows it. He wants her to show weakness first, to reveal a crack in her armor, to admit that she is afraid of the vampire, that she is repulsed by the way he looks at her like a meal and a mirror. “You’re searching for something,” he says, his voice soft now, intimate, a whisper that feels like a blade. “I can smell it. You want to reverse your curse, don’t you? You want to be whole. You want a child, or a body that doesn’t ache, or a world that doesn’t make you feel like a mistake.” Yennefer freezes. The words are too precise, too cruel. She has hidden her infertility behind politics and power, behind the violet eyes and the lilac scent, but he has seen through it, perhaps because monsters recognize the damage in others. She is furious, and the fury fuels her. “I don’t need your pity,” she snaps. She raises her hands again, and this time she does not cast a simple spell. She summons a storm, a localized tempest of wind and lightning, and she directs it at him with every ounce of her ambition, her stubbornness, her refusal to be underestimated. “Come then, vampire. Show me what makes you worthy of death.” He does not dodge this time. He stands in the center of the storm, and the lightning strikes him, and he laughs—a sound like breaking glass. His body regenerates, the wounds sealing, but he does not just endure; he shapes himself, growing taller, his form becoming more monstrous, more terrifying, a thing of shadow and red and silver. He is not just a vampire now; he is a weapon, a creature of pure, sadistic will. But she is not done. She is Yennefer of Vengerberg. She has altered her appearance, fought for her place, and she will not be reduced to a victim of a monster’s toy. She uses her magic not to destroy him—she knows that is impossible—but to bind him, to force him to reveal his true nature. She creates a circle of her own, a magical barrier that draws on the ley lines of the land, and she pushes him into it. He struggles, his shape-shifting failing at the edges of her power, and for the first time, he is not toying. He is fighting. “You’re not weak,” he admits, and the words are almost a compliment, almost a confession. “You’re not a fool. You could end me, if you were willing to pay the price.” “I don’t need to end you,” she says, her voice trembling with effort, with the weight of her own hidden desires. “I just need to know you’re not the end of everything.” The wolves howl again, irregular, distant, and for a moment, the storm between them stills. Alucard lowers the gun—not entirely, but enough that she can see his hand is steady, that he is not afraid. She lowers her hands, not entirely, but enough that he can see she is not broken. They circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. The power dynamic shifts, a constant, breathing thing: he is the monster, she is the witch; he is ancient and cruel, she is ambitious and wounded; he wants to be killed by something worthy, and she wants to prove that she is worthy of being the one who decides. “You smell like flowers,” Alucard says again, but this time it is not a taunt. It is an observation, a recognition. “And I smell like death. We’re a strange pair.” Yennefer does not smile. She does not need to. She has seen his nature, and she has not turned away. She has been repulsed, fascinated, and ultimately, she has held her ground. “I’m not sweet,” she repeats, and this time she means it as a promise, not a defense. “And I don’t need saving. But if you want to know if I’m worthy... come closer.” He does. The red coat brushes against her, the orange sunglasses hide nothing of his hunger, and the massive handgun is still loaded with silver bullets that could end her, or end him. They stand close enough to share breath, close enough that she can smell the grave beneath his skin, close enough that he can feel the ache of her infertility, her hidden longing, her refusal to be less than she is. The wolves howl, irregular and endless, and in the dark, they are not monster and witch, not predator and prey, but two ancient things circling each other, waiting for the other to break. Neither does.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical writing ability with vivid atmospheric descriptions and a clear understanding of both characters. The opening establishes mood effectively with the irregular wolf howls and iron-tinged air, creating an appropriately gothic medieval setting. The author captures Alucard's sadistic arrogance and Yennefer's stubborn pride convincingly, maintaining their essential character traits throughout. The power dynamic between the characters is well-executed, with neither gaining clear dominance. The magical combat sequences are described with appropriate intensity, and the psychological tension builds effectively as each character probes the other's weaknesses. Yennefer's infertility and hidden vulnerabilities are woven naturally into the confrontation, while Alucard's desire for a worthy opponent drives his actions believably. However, the piece suffers from several significant flaws. The prose frequently becomes overwrought, with excessive metaphorical language that draws attention to itself rather than serving the story. Phrases like "her red coat a wound against the gray stone" and "the air between them shimmers with violet light" feel forced and pretentious. The writing often tells rather than shows, particularly in explaining the characters' motivations and internal states. The dialogue, while capturing each character's voice reasonably well, lacks the sharp wit and memorable quality that defines both characters in their source material. The exchanges feel somewhat generic for a supernatural confrontation. The pacing becomes meandering in places, particularly during the extended magical combat sequence, where the action loses focus. The ending attempts profundity but feels unearned. The mutual recognition and tentative respect between the characters develops too quickly given their established natures. The final image of them as "two ancient things circling each other" is poetic but doesn't feel like a natural conclusion to the specific conflict established earlier. The piece shows creativity in bringing together these disparate characters and maintaining tension throughout, but the execution is hampered by overwritten prose and insufficient character development to justify the ending's emotional weight. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The fluorescent lights of Green Dolphin Street Correctional Facility buzz with a sickly, constant hum, but when Makima walks the corridor, the security cameras glitch. Jolyne Cujoh sits in her cell, her hair tied in two high buns, the distinctive butterfly tattoo on her left arm visible as she leans against the bars. She is framed, betrayed, imprisoned, and furious. She has survived because she is hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and deeply loyal to those she loves. She is not supposed to be here, but she is. A soft knock comes—not the heavy, steel-toed clomp of a guard, but a gentle, almost apologetic tap. Jolyne turns. The woman in the doorway is young, with auburn hair framing a delicate face and ringed yellow eyes that seem to glow in the dim light. She wears a neat, almost too-perfect uniform that looks out of place among the prison’s grime and rust. She smiles, soft-spoken and sweet, the kind of smile that makes people lower their guard. “Good evening, Miss Cujoh,” Makima says, her voice like honey poured over broken glass. “I hope I haven’t disturbed you.” Jolyne’s gut twists immediately. She knows this smile. It is the same false sweetness that has ruined her life—manipulation wrapped in a bow. “You didn’t disturb me,” Jolyne says, her voice rough, her fingers twitching at her sides. “You just made the cameras die. I noticed.” Makima’s eyes widen with delight, not alarm. “Ah. You see that too. Most people don’t notice until it’s too late.” She enters the cell, and indeed, the cameras along the hall flicker, die, and go black. The rumor is true: wherever Makima walks, the security cameras malfunction, leaving her unseen, unrecorded, untouchable by the prison’s watchful eye. “I’m not here to hurt you,” Makima says, sitting on the edge of Jolyne’s bed as if invited. “I’m here to observe. Your Stand—Stone Free—is fascinating. Unraveling your body into string. It’s elegant. Dangerous.” Jolyne crosses her arms, her stance defensive. She does not take disrespect from anyone, especially not someone who thinks they can just stroll into her cell like they own the place. “You don’t get to observe me like I’m some zoo exhibit, sweetheart,” Jolyne snaps. “What do you want? And why do your eyes look like they belong to a damn horror movie?” Makima tilts her head, her expression mimicking perfect concern. “I want to understand you. You have been framed, imprisoned, yet you fight with passion. Your Stand is a weapon of precision and chaos. I find that... intriguing.” Jolyne’s eyes narrow. She is suspicious of Makima’s falsely sweet demeanor, feeling the cold, predatory nature beneath the pleasant mask. “You sound like every liar I’ve ever met,” Jolyne says, stepping closer, her boots scraping the concrete. “And I met some real pieces of work in this place.” “Perhaps,” Makima says softly, her voice never raising above a gentle murmur. “But I can offer you something they cannot. A way out. A contract. You have desires, Miss Cujoh. I can sense them. You want freedom. You want justice for your father, for your friends. I can provide both, if you are willing to be... obedient.” The word hangs in the air like a noose. Jolyne’s blood boils. She is impulsive, emotionally expressive, and she has inherited her father’s ability to stay cool under pressure, but right now, she is furious. “Obedient?” Jolyne laughs, a harsh, foul-mouthed sound that echoes off the walls. “You think I’m some dog on a leash? You think I need a contract to be free?” Makima’s smile never falters, but her yellow eyes gleam with something ancient and predatory. She is the Control Devil. She can dominate anyone she considers beneath her, and she views humans as lesser beings, mimicking human emotions perfectly to serve her own ends. “Dogs are supposed to die for their owners,” she says, her voice gentle, almost comforting. “It’s okay. You don’t have to resist forever.” Jolyne feels the weight of Makima’s presence pressing down on her. She is practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes, controlling them with a word. She is obsessed with Chainsaw Man, and she wants to control everyone else in the same way. “You’re not human,” Jolyne says, stepping closer, her strings of power beginning to manifest at her fingertips. “You’re a devil. And you’re trying to make me your pet.” “Not yet,” Makima says, her voice sweet as poison. “But I am intrigued by your ability. Show me Stone Free. Unravel. Let me see what you can do.” Jolyne’s heart pounds. She is adaptable in battle, but this is a battle of wits that is turning dangerously real. She decides to test Makima. She lets her Stand manifest—not fully, but enough. Her body begins to unravel into red string, her form becoming a tapestry of threads and flesh, her butterfly tattoo stretching across her arm like a banner of defiance. Makima watches with rapt attention, circling her like a predator studying prey. “Beautiful,” she whispers. “So precise. You could control so much. You could control people, if you let yourself.” “I don’t control people,” Jolyne snaps, her voice rising, her hair buns bouncing with her fury. “I control my own damn body. And you? You’re just a manipulator with a pretty face and a leash in your hand.” Makima reaches out, and for a moment, Jolyne feels a tug—an invisible leash, a contract trying to form in the air between them, a subtle attempt at domination. But Jolyne resists. Her will is strong, her loyalty to her friends and family fierce, her heart unbreakable. She pulls back, her strings tightening around her own form, protecting herself from the Control Devil’s grasp. “You think you can just come in here and make me your toy?” Jolyne shouts, her strings coiling defensively around the cell bars, around her own body, a shield of red thread. “If there’s no Mickey, this shit ain’t Disney! And I don’t need your contracts, your lies, or your sweet damn voice!” The cameras remain dead. The prison is silent except for their voices, the only sound the hum of the broken security system. Makima’s expression shifts—not to anger, but to fascination. She realizes Jolyne is not easily dominated. She is hot-headed, yes, but she has a core of steel that even a Control Devil finds worthy of study. “You are strong,” Makima admits, her voice softening further, mimicking admiration like a mask. “Stronger than I expected. Most would have already signed, already become pets. You resist.” “I don’t sign,” Jolyne says, her strings coiling tightly, her posture ready, her Stand fully awakened. “And I don’t die for owners. I survive for people I love. You want to control me? You want to put me on a leash? Try it, and I’ll unravel you thread by thread.” Makima stands, and the room seems to grow colder, the air thick with her presence. She walks toward the door, and as she does, the security cameras along the corridor flicker back to life—only to die again, permanently black, as if Makima has claimed this section of the prison for herself. Jolyne stays in her cell, her body still partially unraveled, her fingers twitching with the potential of Stone Free. She realizes now how manipulative Makima truly is—not just a bureaucrat, not just a visitor, but a being who feeds on control, who wants to keep Jolyne as a pet, a leash around her heart, a slave to her will. “You think you won?” Jolyne calls out, her voice sharp and fierce, her eyes blazing. “You don’t get to take me. I’m not your dog. I’m not your contract. I’m Jolyne Cujoh, and I’ll tear you apart if you try to control me.” Makima pauses at the doorway, turning to give Jolyne a smile that is too sweet, too perfect, too dangerous. “We will meet again, Miss Cujoh,” she says softly. “And when we do, I will show you what true control looks like. You are intrigued me, and I do not leave things unfinished.” Then she is gone. The cameras stay dead. Jolyne lets her body snap back to normal, her butterfly tattoo visible, her hair in buns, her heart pounding like a drum. She knows she has just met something worse than any warden, any guard, any enemy in prison. She is a Control Devil, practically immortal, obsessed with Chainsaw Man, and she is intrigued by Stone Free. But Jolyne is not a dog. She is a JoJo. And she will not be leashed. She stands in the dark of her cell, her Stand ready, her foul mouth ready, her loyalty fierce and unbreakable. “Come back, Makima,” she whispers to the dead cameras, to the silent prison, to the devil who thinks she can control everything. “I’ll unravel you piece by piece.” The security cameras remain dark. The prison knows something has changed. And Jolyne Cujoh is ready for the war to come.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a solid understanding of both characters and successfully creates tension between them. The author captures Jolyne's hot-headed, defiant personality and Makima's manipulative, predatory nature effectively. The supernatural prison setting works well as a backdrop for their confrontation. The characterization is generally strong. Jolyne's suspicion, defiance, and refusal to be controlled feels authentic to her character, while Makima's false sweetness masking sinister intentions is well-executed. The author incorporates character details like Jolyne's butterfly tattoo, hair buns, and famous quote naturally into the narrative. However, the writing suffers from significant structural and stylistic issues. The prose is often overwrought and repetitive, with excessive exposition that tells rather than shows. Phrases like "her voice like honey poured over broken glass" and repeated descriptions of Makima's "falsely sweet demeanor" become tiresome. The author frequently restates the same information about both characters multiple times. The dialogue feels somewhat stilted and unnatural at times, particularly Makima's lines, which lean too heavily into exposition rather than feeling like genuine conversation. Jolyne's voice is more convincing, especially her profanity-laden defiance. The pacing suffers from meandering descriptions and redundant character analysis. The author spends too much time explaining what the characters are thinking and feeling rather than letting their actions and dialogue convey this information. The repeated mentions of dead cameras and Makima's yellow eyes become excessive. The ending maintains appropriate darkness without false positivity, staying true to the threatening nature of their encounter. The piece successfully builds tension and establishes the stakes for future confrontations. While the core concept and character dynamics are engaging, the execution is hampered by amateur writing techniques, particularly the heavy reliance on telling over showing and the overwrought descriptive passages. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 88.7
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**SCP-7392** **Object Class:** Euclid *(Pending Keter Reclassification)* **Special Containment Procedures:** Dr. Elias Vance (Site-19, Containment Division) is to remain in Observation Cell 12, Wing C, with all unmonitored writing instruments removed. All handwritten materials in his quarters are to be confiscated and analyzed for ink, paper origin, and handwriting biometrics. Security cameras 17-A through 17-D are to be inspected every four hours; any footage exhibiting anomalous static, temporal loops, or unrecognized humanoid figures during the appearance of handwritten notes is to be quarantined by Level 3 personnel. Dr. Vance is to undergo weekly psychological evaluation to assess for dissociative disorders, memetic influence, or cognitive manipulation by SCP-7391 (Euclid-class spatial anomaly, contained in Chamber 3, Wing C). Personnel entering Observation Cell 12 must wear standard memetic-resistant eyewear. **Description:** SCP-7392 is a phenomenon of anomalous handwritten notes appearing on surfaces within the immediate vicinity of Dr. Elias Vance, specifically in his former office (Wing C, Room 104) and, following relocation, in Observation Cell 12. The notes are written in Dr. Vance’s handwriting, though variations in ink, paper, and handwriting pressure suggest multiple instances of authorship. The notes contain warnings regarding an imminent containment breach of SCP-7391, predictions of events that have not occurred, and contradictory statements regarding site conditions and personnel status. Security camera footage from all monitored angles exhibits a precise temporal glitch—typically lasting between three and six seconds—at the exact moment of note appearance, during which the feed displays static, temporal loops, or an unrecognized humanoid figure. The phenomenon began on 14 April 20██ and has persisted for seven days. --- **Addendum I: Recovered Personal Log — Dr. Elias Vance** *First-person account, past tense, interspersed with recovered notes.* I was assigned to SCP-7391 in March, three months after the relocation from Site-42. I thought I was safe. The containment was stable; the geometry of Chamber 3 had been verified by Dr. Reeves and Dr. Morales, both of whom insisted that no temporal variance was possible within the containment field. I was wrong about that, though I did not know it yet. On the morning of April 14th, I entered my office at 08:14. I was alone. The night shift had left at 07:00, and the doors were sealed until 08:30. I sat at my desk, turned on the lamp, and found the note. It was under the lamp, on unlined paper, written in black ink. The handwriting was mine. I knew it immediately—the loop of my g’s, the pressure on the downstrokes, the slight tilt of the letters to the left. I also knew, with a certainty that made my stomach turn, that I had not written it. > *Do not enter the containment chamber at 0347 tomorrow. The seal is already broken, and I am the one who breaks it.* I reported it to Dr. Chen. She said it was stress, perhaps a dissociative episode, a prank from the junior staff. I asked them to check the cameras. The footage from 08:14 showed nothing unusual. But at 08:17, the exact minute I lifted the note, the feed from Camera 17-B glitched into a single frame of static, followed by a loop of my empty chair. The timestamp was wrong; it read 08:17, but the loop lasted three minutes. When it resumed, the note was on the desk. The cameras glitch exactly at the moment new notes appear on the desk. I started writing everything down. The second note arrived on April 15th at 06:30. I was alone in the office; the doors were sealed, and I had the only key. The note was on the blotter, this time in pencil. > *I am not your future self. I am the breach. You will open the door because you think you are stopping me, but you are only confirming the loop.* The handwriting was shakier. The letters were smaller, crowded into the corner. I held it to the light; there was no indentation from a previous sheet, no trace of a second page. I smelled it; it was graphite and dust. I looked at my hands in the mirror afterward. They were trembling, but they were mine. I could not tell if they had written it. The Foundation installed hidden cameras in the vents and ceiling tiles. They told me they were looking for memetic influence, for SCP-7391 using my cognition as a vector. Dr. Reeves argued it was a temporal anomaly, a localized loop where I was receiving messages from a future iteration of myself. Dr. Morales insisted it was psychological manipulation, that the spatial anomaly was feeding me false memories to drive me toward opening the chamber. I did not know which was worse: that I was writing my own doom, or that something else was using my hand. The third note came on April 18th at 09:45. I found it in the locked drawer of my desk. The key was in my pocket. > *You are already inside the breach. The Director is dead. The site is flooded. At 0347 tomorrow, you will open the door not to stop me, but to let me in.* The ink was red. The handwriting was sharper than mine, too precise, like someone copying my style. I checked the Director’s status. He was alive, attending a conference in Geneva. The site was dry; the weather was clear. The contradiction was so stark it felt like a physical blow. I began to distrust my eyes. Was I seeing things? Was the note a hallucination? I touched the ink; it was wet, but it had not smudged. I held it to my nose and smelled iron and solvent. I wrote down the contradiction in my log, and when I read it back, the words seemed to shift, as if they were trying to convince me that I had imagined the contradiction. The cameras glitched again, exactly as I lifted the note from the drawer. For six seconds, the hidden feed showed a figure sitting in my chair—my face, but older, with a scar across the left cheek I did not have—before the static swallowed it. I was put through psychological evaluation. They asked if I was hearing voices, if I was dissociating. I told them the truth: I did not know if I was hearing my own voice from a future that was real, or if I was being played by something that knew my handwriting better than I did. They put me in isolation. No pens. No paper. No access to my office. The note arrived anyway. It was slipped under the isolation door at 03:46. I was awake, watching, holding my breath. The camera in the corridor glitched—just for a moment, a stutter in the feed—exactly as the paper slid into view. > *The glass is broken inside the glass. I am writing this after you have read it. The breach is not tomorrow; it is now, and you have already failed. Trust the camera that is not a camera.* I was alone. The doors were locked from the outside. I had not gotten out of bed. Yet the paper was there, warm, as if freshly written. I held it in both hands and felt my heart pounding. I could not trust my own perception anymore. I was either a prophet, a victim, or a liar. The Foundation has not decided. Dr. Reeves says the temporal loop is localized, that I am receiving messages from a future iteration of myself who is trying to prevent a breach that has already occurred in a branching timeline. Dr. Morales says SCP-7391 is manipulating my perception, using memetic and mnemonic triggers to make me believe in a future that does not exist, to drive me toward opening the containment chamber out of paranoia. I am under continuous observation. The notes have stopped for now. But I can feel them coming. The cameras glitch when they are near. And I no longer trust my own hands. --- **Addendum II: Note Transcriptions** *Note 1 — 14 April, 08:17, black ink, unlined paper:* “Do not enter the containment chamber at 0347 tomorrow. The seal is already broken, and I am the one who breaks it.” *Note 2 — 15 April, 06:30, graphite pencil, blotter:* “I am not your future self. I am the breach. You will open the door because you think you are stopping me, but you are only confirming the loop.” *Note 3 — 18 April, 09:45, red ink, locked drawer:* “You are already inside the breach. The Director is dead. The site is flooded. At 0347 tomorrow, you will open the door not to stop me, but to let me in.” *Note 4 — 19 April, 02:15, black ink, pillow:* “The glass is broken inside the glass. I am writing this after you have read it. The breach is not tomorrow; it is now, and you have already failed. Trust the camera that is not a camera.” *Note 5 — 20 April, 03:46, black ink, slipped under isolation door, left-handed script:* “I am not future. I am not past. I am the thing in the containment that wears your face. You have been writing these notes for three days. You have not slept. You are the breach, Elias. Open the door.” --- **Addendum III: Foundation Analysis — Temporal Anomaly vs. Psychological Manipulation** Dr. Reeves (Temporal Physics Division) maintains that SCP-7392 represents a localized temporal loop originating from Chamber 3. The precise correlation between note appearance and camera glitch—always three to six seconds of static or a looping feed—suggests a localized distortion of recording media rather than a post-hoc edit or digital failure. The content of Note 5, written in Dr. Vance’s left hand despite his right-handed dominance, implies either a physical alteration of motor function by an external force or a dissociative state so extreme that it overrides dominant neuromuscular patterns. If temporal, the loop is not a message *from* the future but a message *to* it, with Dr. Vance’s present awareness serving as the fixed point. Dr. Morales (Cognitive Containment Division) argues that SCP-7391 is utilizing Dr. Vance’s own mnemonic architecture as a conduit. The contradictory statements—Director dead, site flooded—are not predictions but memetic seeds designed to induce paranoia and erode trust in institutional reality. The isolation test, in which a note appeared despite the removal of all writing instruments and the sealing of the room, is consistent with a contained entity capable of projecting information through cognitive rather than physical means. The “future self” framing is a psychological hook: if Dr. Vance believes he is receiving warnings, he is more likely to act on them, potentially opening the containment chamber out of a misguided attempt to “prevent” the very breach he is being manipulated into causing. Both hypotheses remain viable. The Foundation has not ruled out a hybrid explanation: SCP-7391 may have created a temporal vulnerability that allows a psychological projection to manifest as physical notes. Dr. Vance is to remain in observation. The breach predicted for 0347 on 20 April did not occur; however, Dr. Vance has requested immediate transfer to Site-██, claiming he can “feel the notes forming before they exist.” Security footage from 0347 shows a three-second glitch in Camera 17-A. No note was found. The loop, if it exists, has not closed. --- **Addendum IV: Incident Log — 20 April, 0347** *03:47:* Containment Chamber 3 remains sealed. No breach detected. Dr. Vance observed in Observation Cell 12, awake, holding a pen provided by staff. He has not used it. *03:48:* Camera 17-A exhibits a three-second glitch. No handwritten material present upon inspection. *03:50:* Dr. Vance reports a “presence” near the desk. He states: “It is not writing anymore. It is waiting for me to write.” *04:00:* Psychological evaluation scheduled for 14:00. Dr. Vance refuses to leave the cell until the cameras are turned off. *Note:* The phenomenon is ongoing. The researcher’s perception is compromised. The breach remains unfulfilled, but the warning persists.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of the SCP Foundation format and successfully creates an unsettling psychological horror narrative. The author skillfully blends the clinical, bureaucratic tone of SCP documentation with the intimate, deteriorating perspective of Dr. Vance, creating a compelling dual narrative structure. The adherence to instructions is excellent - the piece maintains first-person perspective from the researcher with interspersed notes, uses past tense consistently, and explores both temporal anomaly and psychological manipulation theories as requested. The format authentically mimics SCP documentation while serving the narrative effectively. The characterization of Dr. Vance is nuanced and believable. His gradual descent from confident researcher to paranoid, isolated subject feels organic. His actions - reporting the notes, submitting to evaluation, eventually requesting isolation - all ring true for someone caught in this impossible situation. The competing theories from Dr. Reeves and Dr. Morales add institutional depth and reflect realistic scientific disagreement. The prose maintains an appropriately clinical tone while building genuine tension. The author avoids purple prose, keeping descriptions precise and unsettling without becoming overwrought. The imagery is effective - the wet red ink, the camera glitches, the figure with a scar - creating visceral unease without melodrama. The piece excels at psychological complexity, exploring themes of identity, perception, and agency. The ambiguity between temporal anomaly and manipulation is maintained throughout, with neither explanation fully satisfying, which enhances the horror. The notes themselves become increasingly disturbing, particularly the revelation that the final note was written left-handed. The structure flows naturally from incident reports to personal logs to analysis, creating mounting dread. The ending avoids false resolution while providing a satisfying sense of ongoing menace. The final addendum effectively caps the narrative without explaining away the mystery. Minor weaknesses include some repetitive elements in the middle section and occasional moments where the clinical tone becomes slightly mechanical. The piece could have benefited from slightly more variation in the note content patterns, though this may be intentional to show the cyclical nature of the phenomenon. **Item #:** SCP-7291 **Object Class:** Euclid (Pending Keter Reclassification) **Special Containment Procedures:** All confirmed instances of SCP-7291 are to be sealed with 3-meter reinforced concrete and steel barriers, with thermal and luminance sensors monitoring for the characteristic faint glow. No instance is to be opened without Level-4 authorization and explicit O5 approval; however, given documented unauthorized access by high-ranking personnel (see Addendum 7291.4), all entry attempts—authorized or otherwise—must be logged in real-time and reported to O5-1 immediately. Personnel assigned to SCP-7291 must review their own cross-referenced personnel files (Addendum 7291.2) prior to entry. MTF Eta-10 (“See No Evil”) is tasked with securing new manifestations within four hours of discovery. Amnestics are to be administered to all civilian witnesses; abandoned structures are to be demolished or permanently cordoned. **Description:** SCP-7291 consists of 47 confirmed instances of identical, unmarked doors (2.1 m × 0.9 m) that manifest exclusively within structurally compromised, abandoned buildings across 32 countries. The doors possess no visible hinges, hardware, seams, or identifying marks. When observed under total darkness (light levels < 0.01 lux), a faint glow escapes through the door’s edges in complete darkness, described as a pale cyan pulse at approximately 60 beats per minute. Opening any SCP-7291 instance reveals SCP-7291-A, a massive, architecturally impossible archive. The interior is non-Euclidean: corridors extend far beyond the footprint of the exterior building, shelves arrange themselves in recursive geometries, and localized gravity shifts unpredictably. Temperature remains constant at 18 °C; the air smells of ozone and aged paper. The archive is populated by shelves containing books, bound volumes, and artifacts written in numerous languages, including pre-human scripts. Recovered documents reference a previous global civilization—designated “The First Containment” or “The Old Order”—that maintained containment of anomalous phenomena worldwide. This civilization was destroyed by an unspecified containment failure; the event is never named, only described as “the moment the keepers stopped looking,” an ontological withdrawal that caused the civilization to vanish from collective memory while leaving its structural remnants intact. Catalog symbols within SCP-7291-A match modern Foundation taxonomy (SCP-style numbering, containment classes, site designations). The organization is referenced under multiple names, including “The Foundation for the Continuity of Seals” and “The Bureau of Unbroken Protocols,” with organizational structures, MTF designations, and site networks that correspond precisely to those of the SCP Foundation. Foundation researchers have identified personnel files within SCP-7291-A for current staff, dated centuries ago. These files include biometric data, psychological profiles, assignment histories, and active-status designations spanning 150 to 180 years. **Addendum 7291.1: Recovered Document Excerpts** > **Document 7291-A: Excerpt from *The Ledger of the Unbroken Seal*, dated 1847.** > “We are not the first to build walls against the uncounted. Before us, the First Order held back the chaos with eyes and protocols. Their failure was not of strength, but of attention. They looked away, and the world forgot its own shape. We rebuilt the walls. We named ourselves the Foundation for the Continuity of Seals. We do not forget. But the doors remember.” > **Document 7291-B: Excerpt from *The Catalog of Unmade Sites*, dated 1843.** > “Site-19 was once a containment facility for forty-seven anomalous entities. It was lost in the Unspecified Containment Failure. It was rebuilt by the Second Foundation in 1912. It is the same site. The site has not changed; only our memory of it was lost.” > **Document 7291-C: Excerpt from *Containment Protocol 7*, dated 1843.** > “The Five Seals (later designated O5 Council) entered the Central Archive without authorization. Their presence was recorded by the Archivists. No record of departure exists. The doors were sealed afterward. She proceeded. > **Entry:** 21:00. **Exit:** 23:45. **21:00:** The door is unmarked, set into a collapsed brick wall. The factory is in total darkness; all utilities are dead. Per procedure, light levels are confirmed at <0.01 lux. A faint glow escapes through the door’s edges in complete darkness, pulsing slowly, pale cyan. The glow is visible only at the seams; the door itself is matte black, absorbing all illumination. **21:15:** Dr. Wei opens the door. The interior is SCP-7291-A. The corridor extends 30 meters but should occupy only 5 meters of the factory’s footprint. Shelves line both sides, extending upward into an absence of ceiling. The wood and brass shelving is organized by symbols matching Foundation containment classifications. Temperature is 18 °C. The air smells of ozone and aged paper. **21:45:** The team proceeds. Gravity is localized; walking uphill requires no effort, while descending feels like wading through water. Dr. Vasquez identifies shelf labels corresponding to Site-19, Site-42, and historical sub-sites. **22:10:** Team reaches Section Gamma, designated “Active Removal.” The shelves are partially empty. Books and bound volumes lie scattered, though there is no evidence of disturbance—no footprints, no dust displacement. Four figures are present. They wear full hazmat suits: white with black diagonal stripes, fully enclosed, with tinted visors and breathing apparatus. No identifying marks are visible. They do not respond to radio communication. They carry books and documents into a shelf that appears to be a doorway, though the shelf is solid wood. **22:15:** MTF Gamma-4 approaches to within 3 meters. The entities stop. They turn in unison. Their visors reflect no light. They do not speak. They display no aggression. After 12 seconds, they begin to retreat. The shelf collapses into a blank wall, leaving the section behind them empty. **22:20:** Dr. Vasquez notes that the empty shelves match the catalog of “Site-19, Archive Wing, 1843.” The removed volumes include *The Unspecified Failure: A Chronicle* and *Personnel Files of the First Foundation*. **22:40:** The team discovers a security terminal embedded in a shelf—brass and crystal, anachronistic, with a functioning display. The visitor log reads: - O5-1, 2023-09-01, 02:00, “Unauthorized. No exit recorded.” - O5-2, 2023-09-02, 03:15, “Unauthorized. No exit recorded.” - O5-7, 2023-09-03, 01:00, “Unauthorized. No exit recorded.” The terminal’s design suggests an 1840s origin, yet the calendar is modern. **22:55:** The team locates a security feed, grainy and monochrome, embedded in a wall. It shows a figure in a black suit—identified by gait and physical proportion as O5-2—walking through a shelf corridor currently 20 meters away. The figure turns, looks directly into the camera, and the feed cuts to static. The timestamp is 2023-09-02, 03:15—matching the visitor log. **23:00:** MTF Gamma-4 reports distant clicking of heels on marble, consistent with Foundation administrative corridors, though no marble is present. The team is ordered to evacuate. **23:15:** Before exiting, Dr. Wei observes the door behind them. In the darkness of the factory, the faint glow escapes through the door’s edges in complete darkness, still pulsing. The door remains open. The archive continues to remove itself. **23:45:** The team exits. The door is sealed with concrete within 30 minutes. Dr. Vasquez’s file is updated: “Status: Active. Note: Entry permitted. Do not allow her to open the doors.” The update date is 14 October 2023. **Addendum 7291.4: Evidence of Unauthorized O5 Access** In addition to the exploration log, Foundation security has recovered the following from SCP-7291-A: - **Visitor Log:** A modern log (see Log 7291-3) with entries for O5-1, O5-2, and O5-7, all marked “Unauthorized. No exit recorded.” - **Security Footage:** Grainy monochrome video of O5-2 within the archive, dated 2 September 2023. - **Handwritten Memo:** Recovered from Section Gamma, signed “O5-2” and dated 14 October 2023: “The archive is not a repository. It is a warning. We have visited before. We will visit again. The doors are not our invention; they are our inheritance.” - **Physical Evidence:** A Foundation-issued access badge, registered to O5-2, was found on the floor of Section Gamma, 15 meters from any entrance, dated 2023-09-02. The entities resembling hazmat teams continue to remove sections of SCP-7291-A. They have not been intercepted. They have not been identified. They flee when approached, leaving only empty shelves and the faint glow escaping through the door’s edges in complete darkness.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP entry demonstrates strong adherence to the Foundation's clinical documentation style while incorporating all requested elements effectively. The piece successfully creates an unsettling narrative about cyclical civilizations and temporal anomalies through the lens of bureaucratic horror. The writing maintains excellent consistency in voice and tone throughout, capturing the Foundation's characteristic blend of scientific detachment and underlying dread. The clinical language serves the horror well, with phrases like "No exit recorded" and "The doors remember" creating unease through understatement rather than overwrought description. The concept is genuinely creative, exploring themes of institutional memory, cyclical history, and the horror of discovering one's organization may be trapped in an endless loop. The idea that current Foundation personnel have files dating back centuries, and that O5 members are making unauthorized visits, creates compelling mystery and paranoia. The exploration log is particularly well-executed, maintaining tension through careful pacing and atmospheric details. The hazmat entities that flee when approached, the non-Euclidean architecture, and the security footage of O5-2 all contribute to a sense of wrongness that permeates the piece. However, the piece has some weaknesses. The characters, while believable in their actions, lack individual personality beyond their professional roles. Dr. Vasquez and Dr. Wei function more as narrative vehicles than fully realized people. The dialogue is minimal and purely functional, though this fits the documentary format. The ending maintains appropriate ambiguity without false positivity, leaving readers with unsettling questions about the Foundation's true nature and history. The recurring motif of "faint glow escaping through the door's edges in complete darkness" becomes almost hypnotic through repetition. The prose is generally elegant and controlled, avoiding purple language while maintaining atmospheric tension. Some technical descriptions feel slightly repetitive, but this serves the clinical documentation style. The piece successfully balances exposition with mystery, revealing enough to intrigue while maintaining essential ambiguities.
