Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The four corner speakers—northwest, northeast, southwest, southeast—blast the same track in perfect synchronization, but the volume is a hair too loud, pushing past music into pure physical pressure. I can feel the bass in my molars, in the bones of my sternum, vibrating the polished wood beneath my worn sneakers. I stand at second row from the mirror, third position from the left, feet shoulder-width apart, knees soft, facing north toward the glass. The studio is a clean rectangle of pine-scented air and mirrored walls, smelling of disinfectant and privilege. I am from the block where streetlights don’t work and dances happen on cardboard over broken concrete, where the air smells of rain on asphalt and fried food. I won this scholarship because I could make my body speak when words failed me. Now I am being asked to make it silent. Instructor Choi stands at the south wall, arms crossed, wearing black. He is famous for breaking students to remake them. He has made trainees weep in this room, then made them perfect. He sees my raw talent—he told me yesterday, in a voice that sounded like a verdict—but he does not see my attitude, my refusal to flatten myself into a point in their grid. The choreography is military. It is not dance; it is architecture with a heartbeat. Count one: I drop. My feet—left sole peeling, right toe scuffed—plant firmly. I bend at the knees until my thighs are parallel to the floor, weight distributed evenly between both legs, spine vertical, shoulders square to the mirror. The choreography demands a sharp *lock*: my right arm bends at exactly ninety degrees, forearm horizontal at shoulder height, hand open with fingers together, thumb aligned with the ceiling. My left hand presses to my left hip, elbow jutting precisely forty-five degrees outward. My head tilts exactly forty-five degrees to the right, eyes fixed on my reflection. But my muscle memory betrays me. Instead of a sharp, isolated snap, I roll through my shoulder. My weight shifts with a slight bounce, a groove born from years of improvising to whatever beat came through the speaker on my block’s corner. I feel the street instinct trying to claim the move, to make it breathe, to turn the mechanical *hit* into something human. Instructor Choi stops the music—not the track, just the room’s rhythm, holding up his hand like a blade. The four speakers continue their synchronized blast, leaving only the hiss of air conditioning and the vibrating bass that shakes the floor. He walks from the south wall to my position. He moves with precision: four steps, each exactly two feet apart, no sway, no bounce, no *groove*. He stops six inches from my left shoulder. “You are not a machine,” he says. His voice is low, precise. “Good. But you are not a street. You must be both, or you will be nothing.” He demonstrates. He is at my position, facing the mirror. He drops into the plié with zero deviation. His arm snaps to the “L” with a sound like a gunshot. He holds it. There is no breath in his body, no sway, no connection between one joint and the next. It is isolation taken to the extreme: head, shoulder, hip, each operating independently, like a puppet with too many strings. Then he points to the center of the studio, to a taped square on the polished wood. “Solo. Center square.” I move. I take three steps—left, right, left—to reach the square in the middle of the room. The others watch from their formations: twelve trainees arranged in three rows of four, two feet apart, all facing north. They wear expensive streetwear, perfect hair, bodies that have been trained since childhood in the precise language of commercial dance. I am the scholarship student, the anomaly, the rough neighborhood kid who slipped through the gate. I begin. Count one: Drop. I force my body into the mechanical shape. Knees at ninety degrees. Right arm in the sharp *L*. Head tilted forty-five degrees right. Count two: Hold. Count three: Hold. Count four: Hold. Count five: Slide. I shift weight to my left foot. My right foot slides exactly twelve inches to the right, landing on the ball of the foot, heel lifted precisely one inch. My right arm extends straight up, index finger pointing to the ceiling, other fingers curled tight. Left hand remains on hip. But my body wants to float. I feel the street in my ankles, the instinct to glide, to make the slide a *glide* rather than a step, to connect the movement with a *top-rock* impulse that wants to rise and fall with the beat. I resist. I keep the heel lifted exactly one inch. Count six: Hold. Count seven: Return. Weight centers over both feet. Right arm drops to a sharp “V” at waist level, palms facing down, fingers together, elbows at exactly forty degrees. Count eight: Freeze. Head snaps to the right, ninety degrees. Eyes fixed on the mirror. Now the turn. Count nine: Pivot. On my left foot, I rotate one hundred eighty degrees to face south—away from the mirror, toward Instructor Choi. My right foot lands at exactly two o’clock relative to my left, knees bent to ninety degrees, thighs parallel to the floor. I drop into a squat. Count ten: Cross. Arms cross tightly at chest, elbows pointing outward, hands flat against my shoulders. No space between my arms and my torso. Count eleven: Hold. Count twelve: Snap back. Pivot on my right foot, rotate to face north, feet together, standing. Now the isolation sequence—the part that breaks me. Count thirteen: Head turns right, sharp, ninety degrees. Hold. Count fourteen: Right shoulder lifts, left shoulder drops. No connection between them. No wave, no roll, no *pop* that connects the joints in a story. Hold. Count fifteen: Right hip pushes out, left hip stays. Hold. My body screams. I want to roll my shoulders together, to connect the head to the neck to the spine in a continuous flow, to make the isolations breathe like a *waacking* sequence that tells the crowd what I feel. Instead, I am a machine. Each part moves alone. Then: The formation shift. From the center square, I must move to my original position—second row, third from left—using only precise steps. Step left with left foot. Step right with right foot, meeting it exactly. No bounce. No *groove*. Arms in “V” at chin height, elbows exactly ninety degrees, fingers together. I take the steps. I feel the music from the southeast speaker—behind me, to my right—vibrating my right shoulder. The northwest speaker, near the mirror, pushes a high-frequency hiss that makes my teeth ache. The four corners are synchronized, but they are too loud, creating a wall of sound that drowns out my own heartbeat, that makes it impossible to hear my own breath. I reach my position. I am in line with the others. We are a grid, a formation of perfect points. Instructor Choi stands at the back wall, watching. “Hold,” he says. “Four counts. Zero movement. Zero breath.” This is the decision point. I am in the “V” position, arms at chin height, feet together, knees soft but locked. The choreography demands I freeze. But my street body wants to breathe. It wants to sway, just a millimeter, to let the *groove* live in my shoulders, to make the freeze not a death but a pause, a breath between battles. I feel my authentic voice—everything I learned on the concrete, the way I made the crowd move with me, the improvisation that saved me when I was hungry—trying to surface, trying to reclaim the space. If I hold perfectly, I will stay. I will have the scholarship. I will become what they want: precise, mechanical, a perfect point in their formation, a tool for their commercial dreams. If I rebel—if I let my shoulder drop, if I let a single beat of my body claim the space, if I insert one *locking* pulse that connects to my heart—I will be expelled. I will lose everything. I will go back to the broken concrete, and this studio will become a memory of failure. My muscle memory betrays me again. My left hand wants to open, to gesture, to ask a question of the mirror. My right knee wants to unlock, to bounce, to remind them that I am alive. I make the choice. I hold. I freeze. My shoulder is locked. My breath is shallow. I am a statue in a grid of statues. The four speakers blast the final beat of the phrase. The bass hits in a synchronized pulse from all four corners—northwest, northeast, southwest, southeast—shaking the floor beneath my feet, vibrating through the bones of my legs, but I do not move. Instructor Choi steps forward. He looks at me. He sees the perfection, and he sees the death in my eyes. “You have done it,” he says. “You are precise. You are correct.” He pauses. “But you have buried your voice.” I look at my reflection. The mirror shows a dancer who is technically perfect, spatially exact, every joint isolated and controlled. The *point choreography* is flawless. The formation is intact. But the person looking back is not me. I have lost the fluidity, the expression, the improvisation that was my only language, my only defense against the world that tried to erase me. The music continues, too loud, too synchronized, too perfect. I realize, with a terror that settles in my stomach like cold concrete, that success here might mean I never dance like myself again. That the scholarship is not just for my body, but for my silence. That to survive in this room, I must become a machine. But I hold the pose. The decision is made. I am still. The room blares. The four corners synchronize. I stand at second row, third from left, facing north, frozen in the “V,” and I feel the cost of every inch of this precision. I have conform. I have survived the rehearsal. I have kept the scholarship. But as the music shakes the walls, I know that somewhere inside my locked shoulders, my buried voice is screaming, and I am not sure if I can ever let it out again without losing everything.

The author maintains meticulous spatial tracking throughout, creating a vivid kinetic map of the studio space with precise positioning (second row, third from left, facing north) and detailed choreographic notation. The physical coherence is remarkable - every movement, from the ninety-degree arm angles to the twelve-inch slide distances, is tracked with mathematical precision while remaining readable. The contrast between street and commercial dance styles is expertly rendered through both technical terminology and physical description. The narrator's muscle memory betrayals feel authentic - the instinct to "roll through my shoulder" instead of hitting sharp isolations, the desire to turn mechanical hits into breathing movements. The collision between fluid street style and militaristic precision creates genuine tension. The first-person voice is consistently maintained with appropriate cultural and class anxiety. The narrator's internal conflict between conformity and authenticity drives the narrative effectively, culminating in a psychologically complex decision that feels earned rather than imposed. The ending avoids false positivity - the protagonist's choice to conform carries real cost, creating emotional complexity. However, the piece occasionally veers toward overwrought description, particularly in the repeated emphasis on speaker positioning and bass vibrations. Some metaphors feel forced ("voice that sounded like a verdict," "arms crossed like a blade"). The dialogue from Instructor Choi, while minimal, feels somewhat stilted and lacks natural speech patterns. The prose generally flows well but sometimes becomes mechanical in its precision, mirroring perhaps too closely the choreography it describes. The emotional engagement is strong, though the relentless focus on technical detail occasionally distances the reader from the character's internal experience. The piece succeeds in creating a genuinely surprising narrative arc - the protagonist's choice to conform rather than rebel subverts expectations while remaining psychologically believable. + Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 81.6
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The hourglass was the only clock that mattered in the Court of the Dreaming, and it was running out of patience. A single, giant vessel of glass dominated the chamber, its shimmering sand falling with a soft, relentless whisper, each grain a tiny dying star. Dream sat behind the bench—impenetrable, eternal, and currently wearing an expression like a man who had just found a cockroach in his wine. He had adjudicated the collapse of empires, the dissolution of nightmares, and the legal separation of a god from his own shadow. Today, he was expected to decide who owned a schoolboy’s almost-kiss. “Call the matter of the Wildflower Field,” Dream said, his voice like velvet over gravel. “Max, aged twelve. Contested by First Love, plaintiff, versus Mora, defendant. Proceed.” First Love stepped forward. Rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful, she wore a dress the color of a blush that had never quite faded. She held a bouquet of wildflowers that seemed to wilt slightly in her presence. “Your Majesty—” she began. “I am not a king,” Dream interrupted, though he did not correct her title with enthusiasm. “Continue.” First Love described the dream. The field. The crush—let us call her Clara, though she was a construct of longing. The muddled almost-kiss. The pleasant confusion of emotions, a feeling like warm honey in a broken jar. It was, she said, a formative experience. A cradle of tenderness. Mora rose from her seat. She was older, Slavic, a figure of paralysis and terror, yet she moved with a strange, unsettling grace, as if she had been carved from the moment before a scream. She wore something close to a nightgown, or perhaps a shroud that had been tailored for a very specific kind of intimacy. “May I present the revised version?” Mora asked, her voice low and practical. Dream sighed, a sound that could have been a wind through a graveyard. “Do.” Mora spoke of the invasion. The field remained, yes. The wildflowers still bloomed, though now they seemed to lean away from the light. The girl—Clara—still mounted the boy, playfully, as if in a game they had both agreed to. But then she morphed. She became terrifying. Attractive, yes, but in the way a cliff is attractive: you want to look, but you know it will kill you. And she sat upon the boy’s chest. She fed on his breath. She caused paralysis. She caused terror. “Is this not an improvement?” Mora asked. “He was bored with the almost-kiss. Now he feels something. He feels terror, which is a kind of love, if you think about it long enough.” First Love turned crimson. “It is not an improvement! It is a parasitic occupation! The boy’s formative experience is now a feeding session!” “Objection!” Mora called out, though no one had objected. “The plaintiff is merely jealous because she cannot feed.” Dream’s eyes narrowed. Not because Mora was wrong, but because he was tired of the case. “Evidence?” The bailiff—an entity that looked like a filing cabinet with eyes—produced a vial of breath, shimmering and slightly blue. It was labeled: Max, 3:47 AM, second week of March. “Exhibit A,” Mora said, “is the breath I have consumed. Exhibit B is the paralysis, which I have documented. Exhibit C—” she produced a wildflower, “—is the flower that grew in his mouth after I sat on him. I am not destroying the dream. I am expanding it.” First Love wept, though her tears were rose-colored and smelled of vanilla. “The almost-kiss was meant to be muddled, not monstrous! The confusion was pleasant! Now he is confused because he is terrified of his own heart!” “Your Majesty,” Mora said, turning to Dream with a practical smile, “a girl’s gotta eat too, you know?” Dream felt a flicker of irritation—not at Mora, but at the absurdity of having to weigh romantic copyright against respiratory rights. He considered the precedents. There was the case of the Nightmare of the Unfinished Letter, where a grief spirit had been granted squatter’s rights because she had slept in a letter for three centuries. There was the matter of the Dream of the Burning Library, where a fire spirit had been evicted because she had not filed her emotional taxes. But this was different. This was a schoolboy. This was first love. Dream looked at the hourglass. The sand was falling faster now, as if the universe itself was impatient. “I will hear final arguments.” First Love spoke of emotional integrity, of the sanctity of formative experience, of the wildflower field as a sanctuary. Mora spoke of hunger. “He breathes, I breathe. It is ecology. The dream is a landscape, and I am the predator that makes it real. Without me, he is just a boy lying in flowers. With me, he knows what it is to be consumed by desire. This is education.” Dream felt the mischief rising. It was not often that he was tempted to mischief in court. Usually, he was impartial, cold, a mirror that reflected only the law of dreams. But here, the law seemed too small, and the absurdity too large. “You make a practical argument,” Dream said, leaning forward. “And you make a terrible one.” “Thank you,” Mora said. “I find that you have established a possessory interest through continuous occupation and respiratory consumption,” Dream said. “The wildflowers, however, remain the property of First Love, as they were planted in the soil of her intent.” First Love nodded, hopeful. “Therefore,” Dream continued, “I rule that Mora may remain in the dreamscape. She may sit upon the boy’s chest. She may feed upon his breath. She may cause paralysis and terror, and she may maintain her confusing attractiveness.” First Love’s hope faltered. “However,” Dream said, with a smile that was not kind, “First Love is hereby appointed as the dream’s emotional consultant, and she must remain present at all times, wearing her wildflowers, and she must blush continuously during the feeding. Furthermore, Mora, you are ordered to say, at least once per dream cycle, that a girl’s gotta eat too, you know?” Mora was silent. “But here is the mischief,” Dream said, and the hourglass seemed to shudder. “The almost-kiss is not removed. It is preserved, but it is now interrupted. Every time the girl mounts the boy, she will morph—not into Mora, but into both of them, at once. The boy will feel the pleasant confusion of First Love, and the terror of Mora, and he will not know which is which. His crush will never be fully realized, because the dream will now be a perpetual almost-kiss that is also a perpetual feeding. You have not stolen the dream, Mora. You have made it eternal. And First Love, you must watch your work become a horror, and you must blush while it happens, because that is your job now.” First Love looked horrified, but also, faintly, pleased. It was, after all, still an emotional experience. Mora considered. “Can I at least have the breath?” “You may have the breath,” Dream said. “But you must lie in the wildflowers while you take it. And you must apologize to them.” The court was silent. Dream stood, or seemed to, for he was not exactly a man, and he looked at the hourglass. The sand had nearly fallen. “This court is adjourned. The boy will dream of terror and tenderness, and he will wake confused, which is the point of all dreams. Mora, you have won a tenancy. First Love, you have lost your solitude. And I have lost an afternoon to a schoolboy’s respiration. May all of you find what you seek.” As the parties left, Mora turned to First Love with a practical shrug. “A girl’s gotta eat,” she said again, but this time with a touch of respect. First Love blushed, and the wildflowers in her hair turned slightly darker, as if they had heard something they did not like. Dream watched them go, and for a moment, the impenetrable mask slipped—not into anger, but into a very small, very dark amusement. The hourglass turned, and the sand began to fall again, counting down to the next case, and the next, and the next, until the dreams themselves grew tired of being owned.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt's requirements, successfully creating a dark fantasy courtroom scene with comedic elements set in Neil Gaiman's Dreaming universe. The author captures Dream's characteristic voice and demeanor effectively, portraying his irritation at adjudicating such mundane matters while maintaining his otherworldly gravitas. The characterizations are well-executed and nuanced. Dream's impenetrable facade cracking into "very small, very dark amusement" feels authentic to the character. First Love is portrayed with appropriate bashfulness and romantic idealism, while Mora's practical, matter-of-fact approach to her parasitic nature ("a girl's gotta eat too, you know?") creates effective dark comedy. The contrast between their motivations drives both conflict and humor naturally. The prose style is elegant and controlled, avoiding purple prose while maintaining atmospheric richness. Descriptions like "his voice like velvet over gravel" and "each grain a tiny dying star" establish mood without overwhelming the narrative. The author uses descriptive language sparingly as requested, focusing on character interaction and dialogue. The dark humor emerges organically from the absurd situation - a cosmic entity forced to adjudicate a schoolboy's romantic dreams. The comedy feels earned rather than forced, particularly in Dream's mischievous resolution that satisfies neither party while creating an even more complex situation. The resolution demonstrates creativity and understanding of Dream's character. Rather than a simple ruling, Dream crafts a punishment that reflects his irritation while maintaining cosmic balance. The ending where both entities must coexist in an eternal, confused state mirrors the complexity of adolescent emotions effectively. The dialogue feels natural and character-appropriate. Mora's repeated practical justifications, First Love's romantic protestations, and Dream's formal yet increasingly irritated responses all ring true to their natures. The piece maintains coherent internal logic within the fantastical setting, and the pacing moves efficiently through courtroom proceedings without meandering. The emotional complexity emerges through the layered resolution that transforms simple territorial dispute into commentary on the nature of formative experiences. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the humor could be more understated, and the ending, while creative, borders on being overly complex. However, these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 77.2
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The broken cart wheel lies abandoned near the village gates, its wooden rim splintered into jagged teeth, the iron axle snapped clean through. Mud and panic cling to the ruts; someone fled in a hurry, leaving behind a single leather strap that dangles like a severed limb. Alucard stands beneath the arch, his red coat a slash of arterial color against the grey stone. He wears his wide-brimmed hat low, and behind the orange sunglasses, his eyes gleam with predatory amusement. In his gloved hands he cradles a massive handgun, the barrel thick enough to be a cannon, loaded with silver bullets that could kill a werewolf, that could hurt him if he allows it. He is not alone. Yennefer of Vengerberg materializes at the edge of the square, her violet eyes narrowing at the vampire. She smells of lilac and gooseberries, a scent that clashes violently with the copper and old blood in the air. She has altered her appearance with such precision that no one sees the hunchback she once was; her posture is perfect now, her face beautiful and severe, but the power beneath her skin is ancient, stubborn, and utterly unwilling to bow. She is centuries old, ambitious, politically savvy, and she has no patience for fools. “You’re the reason the cart ran,” she says. Her voice is sharp, sarcastic, cutting through the damp air. Alucard turns. His smile is a blade. “Perhaps. Or perhaps the cart simply couldn’t bear the weight of its own cowardice. The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame.” He raises the handgun, not pointing directly, just letting the silver glint in the failing light. She doesn’t flinch. “I’m not sweet, and I’m not a maiden in distress in need of saving. You can put the toy down, monster.” He laughs, a sound like breaking glass. “Monster? You say that with such disgust, yet you haven’t fled. Most mortals run. Most sorceresses scream.” “I don’t scream,” she says, and her hands move. A circle of fire erupts around him—not to burn, but to test. He steps through it, his coat unharmed, his body regenerating any scorch marks instantly. He is ancient, immensely powerful, and he takes pleasure in the game. She feels the fascination creeping in despite herself. His monstrous nature—the way he doesn’t bleed, the way he can shape-shift at will, the arrogance of his posture—repels her. She is a woman who rebuilt her body from a hunchback, who altered her face to hide scars, who knows what it is to be monstrous in one’s own way. She is repulsed by his lack of humanity, yet she is drawn to the raw, unfiltered power he carries. He is a mirror she refuses to look into. “Your fire is weak,” Alucard says, and he moves faster than she expects. He doesn’t attack with the gun; he uses it as a prop, a statement of intent. He closes the distance, his red coat swirling, and he is suddenly beside her, close enough that she smells the grave on him, the centuries of death, the cold of the void he carries inside. She casts a spell—an ice shard, a binding sigil that seeks to constrict his limbs. He catches the ice in his hand, and the sigil dissolves against his skin. He is a vampire; he despises weak vampires, but he respects strength. She has it. “You’re not afraid of me,” he says, his voice low, almost intimate. “I am afraid,” she admits, and her violet eyes flash with anger and something else—fascination, perhaps, or the recognition of an equal. “But fear is a tool. You think you can toy with me? You seek worthy opponents. I am not your plaything.” The power dynamic shifts. She is the sorceress, the political mastermind, the one who has survived centuries by manipulation and will. He is the vampire, the predator, the one who kills for pleasure and seeks an end to his immortal existence. They circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. He shape-shifts subtly—his arm elongates, his fingers becoming claws, testing her reflexes. She dodges, her body moving with magical grace, and she strikes back with a blast of pure force that sends him skidding backward into the broken cart wheel. The wood shatters further, splinters flying like white bones. Alucard stands, unharmed, and he is grinning now, truly delighted. “Good. You can take a hit. You can fight back. Most of your kind are either too weak or too arrogant to survive a conversation with me.” “I’ve survived worse than you,” she snaps, and she raises her hands, weaving a complex spell—one that binds, that constrains, that seeks to trap him in a cage of pure will. For a moment, he is caught. His red coat flickers, his sunglasses reflect her violet eyes, and for the first time, he feels a flicker of something other than amusement: respect. But he is a vampire of immense power. He breaks the cage with a roar of sound, not a scream, but a thunderclap of ancient fury. The broken cart wheel spins wildly, the village gates tremble, and the muddy ground cracks beneath their feet. “You want to reverse your infertility,” he says suddenly, his voice cutting through the chaos. He knows her secrets, or he guesses them—he is ancient, he reads people like books, and he sees the desperation beneath her cold exterior, the way she touches her own face as if checking for flaws, the way she speaks of legacy with a hunger that borders on grief. She freezes. “What?” “You want to be whole. You want to be a mother, or at least not broken. And I...” He opens his coat slightly, showing the monstrous nature beneath—scars, darkness, the thing that is not human, the hunger that never dies. “I want to be dead. We are both seeking something impossible.” The power dynamic shifts again. She is vulnerable, and he has seen it. But she is not weak. She steps closer, her smell of lilac and gooseberries mixing with the grave air, and she touches his face—not with affection, but with a challenge that burns. “Then let’s see which of us breaks first,” she says. He doesn’t move away. He lets her touch him. He is fascinated by her refusal to be repulsed, by her willingness to face the monster head-on. She is repulsed by his nature, yes, but she is also fascinated by the power that could end her, by the possibility that he might be the one worthy of her time, worthy of her loyalty, worthy of the deep love she rarely shows. “I could kill you,” he says softly. “You could try,” she replies. They stand there, in the shadow of the village gates, beside the broken cart wheel that speaks of a hurried departure, neither showing weakness, neither backing down. The sun sets, and Alucard’s sunglasses hide his eyes, but Yennefer sees the truth: he wants her to fight, to survive, to be worthy. And she sees in his monstrous nature not just death, but a kind of terrible, beautiful freedom that she has never allowed herself to want. She lowers her hands, but she doesn’t lower her guard. “Again,” she says. He raises the handgun, silver bullets glinting like teeth, and she raises her hands to weave. The power dynamic is not settled. It never will be. But for now, they are equals in the dark, and that is enough.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and character understanding while delivering an atmospheric encounter between two iconic characters. The author successfully captures the essence of both Alucard and Yennefer, maintaining their distinctive voices and power dynamics throughout the confrontation. The opening imagery is particularly effective, using the broken cart wheel as both atmospheric detail and metaphor for the disruption these powerful beings bring to ordinary life. The prose maintains a consistent dark, gothic tone that suits both characters and the medieval European setting. The author skillfully weaves in character-specific details like Alucard's red coat and massive handgun, Yennefer's violet eyes and scent of lilac and gooseberries, creating vivid sensory experiences. The dialogue feels authentic to both characters, capturing Alucard's sadistic playfulness and philosophical nature alongside Yennefer's sharp wit and refusal to be intimidated. The incorporation of their signature quotes feels natural rather than forced. The power dynamic shifts are well-executed, showing neither character as definitively superior, which maintains tension throughout. However, the piece suffers from some overwrought passages, particularly in the middle sections where metaphors become heavy-handed ("fear is a tool," the repeated mirror imagery). Some descriptions veer toward purple prose, especially when describing Alucard's monstrous transformations and the magical confrontations. The pacing occasionally slows due to overly elaborate descriptions that could be more concise. The emotional complexity is strong, particularly in exploring Yennefer's fascination despite her revulsion, and Alucard's respect for a worthy opponent. The revelation about Yennefer's infertility and Alucard's death wish adds psychological depth, though it feels somewhat abrupt when introduced. The ending maintains the tension appropriately without forcing resolution, staying true to the prompt's requirement that neither character show weakness first. The circular structure, returning to combat readiness, works well thematically. + Fanfic-crossover: Prison Strings — Score: 78.4
Prompt:
Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is. **Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)** Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The chain-link fences within the yard rattle whenever an inmate passes by, and right now they scream like a choir of broken bones. Jolyne Cujoh walks with her chin up, her two buns pinned tight against her scalp, the butterfly tattoo on her left arm visible beneath the torn sleeve of her prison jumpsuit. She is innocent, framed for murder, and she knows it with the kind of certainty that burns in her chest like a second heart. The supernatural prison facility is not made of ordinary stone; the walls breathe with a dull, hungry pulse, and the guards are not human. They are devils in cheap uniforms, and they watch her with yellow-ringed eyes that seem to memorize her every breath. She stops when she feels it—a presence that smells like sugar, rust, and something older than the prison itself. Makima stands at the gate, auburn hair framing a face that could belong to a doll or a predator. Her eyes are yellow with black rings, and she smiles with a softness that makes Jolyne’s teeth grind together. "Miss Cujoh," Makima says, her voice like warm syrup poured over ice. "I’ve been hoping to meet you." Jolyne doesn’t move. Her hand rests near her hip, close to where Stone Free waits beneath her skin. "You got the wrong girl, sweetheart. I don’t do meetings. I don’t do pretty faces. And I sure as hell don’t do visitors who think they can waltz into a prison and act like they own the air." "I’ve heard of Stone Free." Makima steps closer, and the chain-link fences rattle again, though no one else is near. "Your ability to unravel yourself into string... it’s fascinating. So precise. So controllable. You can become anything, and yet you remain exactly yourself." Jolyne’s hand twitches. She doesn’t hide her Stand; she never hides it. The string is her weapon, her shield, her proof that she can break apart and still hold together. "You want to know if I can tie you up?" "I want to understand you." Makima tilts her head, and for a moment her smile wavers, just slightly, revealing something cold and ancient behind it, something that has watched civilizations burn. "You’re hot-headed, foul-mouthed, impulsive. You inherited your father’s coolness but wear your heart on your sleeve. You’re loyal to a fault. And yet... you’re here, in a place where loyalty is just another leash, and love is just another contract." Jolyne feels the hair on her neck stand up. The word "contract" hits her like a physical blow. "What are you?" "A visitor." Makima’s eyes gleam with a light that is not human. "But I can offer you more than this cage. I can offer you purpose. Your Stand is rare. I have contracts for those who are... exceptional." "Contracts?" Jolyne laughs, harsh and loud, the sound echoing off the breathing walls. "You think I’m some dog you can leash? You think I’m going to sign away my soul because you showed up with a pretty smile?" Makima’s smile doesn’t falter, but her voice drops to a whisper that cuts through the yard’s noise, sharp and intimate. "Dogs are supposed to die for their owners. It’s okay." Jolyne’s face burns with a rage that is almost holy. "If there’s no Mickey, this shit ain’t Disney!" she snarls, stepping forward until she is inches from Makima’s perfect face. "You come here with your auburn hair and your ringed eyes, trying to wrap me in your bullshit like I’m some string puppet? I’m not your pet. I’m not your contract. I’m Jolyne Cujoh, and I don’t take disrespect from anyone—not from guards, not from devils, not from you. I don’t need your sweet lies. I need out." She unravels her arm. Stone Free bursts from her shoulder, not as a weapon but as an extension of her fury. The string whips out, thick and white, and Jolyne controls it with a flick of her wrist that is pure instinct. It coils around Makima’s wrist—not tight enough to hurt, but enough to stop her from stepping closer, enough to say: *I see you.* Makima looks down at the string, then up at Jolyne, and for the first time her expression shifts—not to anger, but to genuine, terrifying intrigue. "You resist," she says softly. "Most would already feel the weight of my offer. The desire to be seen, to be important, to be saved from this place. You have such a strong will. It makes you... valuable." "I don’t want your save," Jolyne spits, her voice trembling with the effort of holding back her temper. "I want out. And I want to know why you’re really here. What do you want from me?" Makima pulls gently, and the string slides off her wrist as if it were silk, leaving no mark, no scar, only the faint smell of sugar. "I’m here because you’re different," she says. "Your ability to unravel—to become something else while remaining yourself—is unique. I collect unique things. I have many pets in this facility, Jolyne. Inmates who have signed contracts for freedom, for power, for love. They wear leashes that you cannot see, but they feel them every second. And they serve me because they believe it is their choice." Jolyne’s eyes narrow. She looks past Makima, and suddenly she sees them: inmates sitting in the yard, their eyes glazed, their movements synchronized, each one connected by invisible threads to a central point where Makima stands. The chain-link fences rattle violently, not from wind, but from the tension of their controlled bodies, from the invisible strings pulling them in unison. "You’re the Control Devil," Jolyne says, her voice steady now, cold and sharp as a blade. "You don’t care about me. You just want to add me to your collection. You want to make me one of your pets." "I care about potential," Makima corrects, but her yellow eyes flash with something predatory, something that has devoured gods. "You could be so much more if you stopped fighting. If you let me see you... truly." Jolyne’s string wraps around her own body, protecting her heart, her mind, her loyalty to her father, her friends, the people she swore to protect. She thinks of Stone Free not as a tool for control, but as a weapon for freedom, for the right to choose her own strings. "You think you can manipulate everyone," Jolyne says, stepping closer, her string tightening into a blade-sharp edge that glints in the dim light. "You think sweetness is a trap, and maybe it is. But I’m not some weak little thing you can wrap up with promises of power. I’ve been framed, I’ve been imprisoned, and I’ve survived because I don’t bow to people who think they’re gods. You want to control me? Try." She strikes—not at Makima’s body, but at the invisible threads that connect the inmates. Her string slices through them, one by one, and the prisoners shudder, blinking, their eyes clearing as they realize they are free, that the leash is gone. The chain-link fences rattle violently, a deafening chorus of metal screaming against metal, because the prisoners are moving, running, breaking, the invisible strings snapping like wet paper. Makima’s smile finally falters. "You shouldn’t have done that," she says, and for the first time her voice carries a hint of something other than sweetness—something like fear, or respect, or the cold realization that she has met her match. Jolyne stands her ground, her string coiled like a serpent around her arm, her butterfly tattoo visible, her hair still in its defiant buns. "I don’t need your contracts. I don’t need your leashes. I don’t need you to tell me who I am or what I’m worth." Makima steps back, her auburn hair whipping in the wind of the chaos, her yellow eyes narrowing to slits. "You’re a fool, Jolyne Cujoh. You could have been powerful. You could have been mine." "I’m already powerful," Jolyne says, and she means it with every fiber of her being. "And I’m not yours. I’m not anyone’s." The fences rattle one last time as Makima vanishes—not with a flash, but with a whisper, leaving behind only the scent of sugar and rust, and a single black thread that Jolyne catches in her hand. She looks at it, then burns it with her Stand’s heat, watching it turn to ash. She is still in prison. But she is not controlled. She is Jolyne Cujoh. And she will not be a dog.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong character work and atmospheric writing, successfully capturing the essence of both Jolyne and Makima while creating a tense supernatural prison setting. The author shows clear understanding of both characters' core traits and motivations, translating them effectively into prose. The characterization is particularly strong. Jolyne's hot-headed defiance, loyalty, and refusal to be controlled comes through authentically, while Makima's manipulative sweetness masking predatory control is well-executed. The dialogue feels natural to both characters, especially Jolyne's crude directness and Makima's deceptively gentle manipulation attempts. The prose quality is generally high, with evocative imagery like "walls breathe with a dull, hungry pulse" and "chain-link fences rattle like a choir of broken bones." The writing maintains consistent third-person present tense throughout and creates a genuinely unsettling atmosphere appropriate to the supernatural prison setting. However, the piece suffers from some overwrought moments and occasional purple prose. Phrases like "rage that is almost holy" and extended metaphorical descriptions sometimes feel excessive. The climactic scene where Jolyne cuts through Makima's control threads, while thematically appropriate, happens rather quickly and could have used more buildup. The story structure works well as a character study and confrontation piece, though it's more of a single scene than a complete narrative arc. The ending feels earned rather than artificially positive - Jolyne remains imprisoned but maintains her autonomy, which fits both her character and the situation. The writing shows technical competence with good sentence flow and minimal meandering. The author successfully balances action, dialogue, and internal character work without losing focus. While not groundbreaking in concept, the execution elevates familiar character dynamics into something engaging. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-7491 **Object Class:** Euclid **Special Containment Procedures:** Dr. Elias Vance (Site-19, Containment Division / Temporal Studies) is to remain under continuous observation in Quarters 14-B, Wing C. All paper products entering his quarters must be screened for unauthorized ink. He is permitted one standard-issue pen for documentation; all handwritten materials produced or discovered are to be collected at end of shift and stored in a sealed container (SCP-7491-Storage). Security is to be alerted if SCP-7491-A instances contain references to future containment events at Site-19. Dr. Vance is not to be left unsupervised with SCP-████ (the entity under review) for more than fifteen minutes. Psychological evaluation is mandatory every seventy-two hours. If Dr. Vance exhibits signs of dissociation or claims to have written material he does not recall, he is to be sedated and moved to Observation Ward 3. **Description:** SCP-7491 is a series of handwritten notes (SCP-7491-A through SCP-7491-F) recovered from Dr. Elias Vance’s office and residence between March 14 and March 29, 20XX. The notes are written on standard Site-19 copy paper, in Dr. Vance’s handwriting, using ink that does not match any pen in his possession, any inventory item, or any commercial supplier available to the Foundation. The content describes a future containment breach at Site-19 involving SCP-████, an entity currently secured in Sublevel 4. The notes increase in urgency, incoherence, and contradiction of observable reality. Dr. Vance claims to have found them at irregular intervals, often in locations he had not visited, and denies writing them, though handwriting analysis confirms they are his. **Addendum 7491.1 — Recovered Log of Dr. Elias Vance** I found the first note on Tuesday morning, March 14. I had been reviewing containment logs for SCP-████ for three hours when I noticed a scrap of paper on my desk—just a half-sheet, folded once, tucked under my coffee mug. The handwriting was mine, but I didn’t remember writing it. It said: *Don’t open the secondary seal on Thursday. The breach isn’t here yet, but the ink knows. Trust the paper.* I laughed. I was tired. The secondary seal was a routine maintenance check scheduled for Thursday at 0400, and I had already approved it. I threw the note in the recycling. I told myself it was a prank from the junior staff, or perhaps a leftover reminder from a previous shift. The second note was in my coat pocket when I arrived on Thursday. I hadn’t worn that coat since Monday; it had been hanging in my locker, untouched. It was written in the same ink—black, slightly smudged at the edges, though I had never used a fountain pen in my life and had no access to one. It said: *The doors failed at 0400. I am writing this from the other side of the breach. The entity isn’t in the cell; it’s in the notes. They are using me to warn you because I am the only one who can write.* I checked the containment chamber. The doors were sealed. The cameras showed no breach. The time was 0415. Nothing had failed. I told Dr. Reeves, my supervisor in Temporal Studies, that I thought someone was trying to unnerve me before the maintenance check. He said he would investigate the staff. He found nothing. The third note was pinned to my monitor with a paperclip I didn’t own. It was longer, and the handwriting was tighter, more frantic, the letters compressed as if written in a hurry or in darkness. *The sky is green outside. The walls breathe. You are not in Site-19 anymore. The breach already happened because I wrote this.* I looked at the wall. It was concrete. It did not breathe. There is no window in my office; the sky is not visible, and even if it were, it was a clear gray morning. I checked my location on the Site map. I was in Wing C, Office 14-B. I was in Site-19. But I could smell copper, and the air felt thick, as if the room were holding its breath. By the fifth note, I was not laughing. **Addendum 7491.2 — Note Transcripts (Selected)** *Note 7491-A (March 14):* Don’t open the secondary seal on Thursday. The breach isn’t here yet, but the ink knows. Trust the paper. *Note 7491-B (March 16):* The doors failed at 0400. I am writing this from the other side of the breach. The entity isn’t in the cell; it’s in the notes. They are using me to warn you because I am the only one who can write. *Note 7491-C (March 18):* The sky is green outside. The walls breathe. You are not in Site-19 anymore. The breach already happened because I wrote this. *Note 7491-D (March 21):* You are not the first to read this. You are the last. The breach already happened because I wrote this. The Director is dead. The chamber is open. Check the cameras—they are lying. *Note 7491-E (March 24):* I am writing this with my left hand. I am right-handed. The ink is proof, but proof is just a word for fear. The containment failed because I failed. The notes are eating time. *Note 7491-F (March 29):* You are the breach. The containment failed because I failed. The ink is proof, but proof is just a word for fear. Don’t trust me. Don’t trust the paper. Burn it. **Addendum 7491.3 — Foundation Assessment and Ink Analysis** Dr. Reeves from Temporal Studies interviewed me on March 20. He wanted to know if this was a temporal loop—if I was receiving information from a future version of myself that had experienced the breach. He asked me to predict the exact minute of the failure. The notes said Thursday at 0400, but Thursday passed. The doors held. The cameras showed nothing. If it was a temporal anomaly, the breach should have occurred, or should occur, in a way that was verifiable. It wasn’t. Dr. Reeves concluded that a pure temporal explanation was unsupported by evidence, though he admitted the notes’ predictive framing was unusual. Then Dr. Chen from Psychological Containment arrived. She told me that SCP-████ has documented memetic properties—subtle, but present. It can influence perception, induce paranoia, and, in rare cases, manipulate physical media within its containment zone. She suggested that the entity might be using my own cognitive patterns to generate the notes, essentially writing through me as a vector. She asked if I had been alone with the entity recently. I had. I had been in the observation chamber for twenty minutes on March 19, longer than protocol allowed because I was reviewing a data discrepancy that I now cannot recall. The ink analysis came back on March 22. The results were ambiguous, which was worse than conclusive. The ink contained a synthetic polymer not manufactured since 2087, and trace elements of a compound designated “chroniton residue”—a marker sometimes associated with temporal displacement. However, it also contained a psychotropic alkaloid that matched secretions recovered from SCP-████’s containment chamber. The Foundation could not determine if the notes were a temporal artifact or a biological manipulation. The handwriting was mine. The paper was standard. The ink was impossible. Dr. Chen told me that my perception was compromised. She pointed out that Note 7491-D claimed the Site Director was dead, but he had eaten lunch in the cafeteria that same day, laughing with the security staff. Note 7491-E claimed the chamber was open, but the cameras showed it sealed, the locks engaged, the temperature stable. I was told to take leave. I refused. I told them I could tell the difference between a delusion and a warning, but I was beginning to doubt whether that distinction still existed for me. **Addendum 7491.4 — Final Entry (Recovered from Quarters 14-B)** I started to distrust my own hands. I would find ink on my fingers and not know when it got there. I wrote a memo to confirm I was sane, and when I read it back, the words were different—my handwriting, but the sentence said: *The breach is already inside you.* I tore it up. I told Dr. Reeves I was fine. I wasn’t. The notes became increasingly desperate. Note 7491-E was written in my handwriting but with my left hand—I am right-handed, and I have never written with my left hand except to hold a coffee cup. The paper was soaked in something that smelled like the containment chamber: ozone, copper, old stone. It said: *I am not writing this. I am reading it. The future is a trap made of paper. The breach is me.* The sixth note was in my pocket after I woke up in Observation Ward 3. I don’t remember being sedated. I don’t remember how long I had been there. The note was short. It was written in the same impossible ink. *You are the breach. The containment failed because I failed. The ink is proof, but proof is just a word for fear. Don’t trust me. Don’t trust the paper. Burn it.* I looked at the ink. It was the same. Unmatched. Unexplainable. I don’t know if I wrote it, or if I will write it, or if it is already written. I don’t know if the breach is coming, or if it is already here, hidden in the notes, hidden in my own perception. The Foundation has the papers now. They are sealed. They say it is psychological manipulation. They say it is not temporal. They say I am unreliable. But the ink is still on my fingers. And I can still smell copper. **End Log.** **Status:** Dr. Vance remains under observation. SCP-7491-A through F are stored in a sealed container at Site-19. The origin of the notes—whether temporal feedback, memetic influence by SCP-████, or an unclassified phenomenon—remains undetermined. Dr. Vance has been reassigned to administrative review pending psychological clearance. A new note was found in his observation room this morning. It was blank, except for a single word in the same ink: *Burn.*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of the SCP Foundation format and successfully creates an unsettling psychological horror narrative. The author skillfully blends the clinical, bureaucratic tone of SCP documentation with the increasingly desperate first-person perspective of Dr. Vance, creating a compelling contrast that enhances the horror elements. The structure is well-executed, moving from standard containment procedures through increasingly disturbing note transcripts to personal log entries. The progression from rational skepticism to paranoid uncertainty feels authentic and earned. The author maintains the SCP format conventions while allowing the narrative voice to deteriorate alongside the protagonist's mental state. The central mystery—whether the notes represent temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation—is handled with appropriate ambiguity. The Foundation's investigation feels realistic, with multiple departments offering competing theories based on their expertise. The ink analysis providing contradictory evidence (future compounds mixed with psychotropic substances) is a particularly clever touch that maintains uncertainty. Character development is subtle but effective within the constraints of the format. Dr. Vance's transformation from confident researcher to paranoid observer feels gradual and believable. His growing distrust of his own perceptions is well-portrayed through specific details like finding ink on his fingers and the left-handed writing despite being right-handed. The imagery is consistently unsettling without becoming overwrought. Details like the copper smell, the impossible ink, and the breathing walls create atmosphere without excessive description. The prose maintains clinical precision while allowing moments of genuine dread to emerge. **Item #:** SCP-7391 **Object Class:** Euclid **Special Containment Procedures:** Foundation webcrawlers and regional agents are to monitor global reports of unmarked doors discovered in derelict structures. Upon identification, the door (designated SCP-7391-##) is to be sealed with reinforced steel plating, concrete grout, and continuous video surveillance. Amnestic treatment is to be administered to all witnesses. No personnel below Level 4 clearance may enter SCP-7391-A without written authorization from at least two members of the O5 Council; however, it is noted that this authorization has never been granted for any exploratory mission to date, and all evidence suggests that certain Council members have bypassed this protocol independently. All exploration of SCP-7391-A requires a minimum team of four, including one MTF unit equipped for non-Euclidean navigation and one archivist. Teams are to carry recording devices, biometric scanners, and physical markers to track spatial displacement. If entities resembling Foundation HAZMAT personnel are encountered, teams are instructed to observe from a minimum distance of 15 meters, document all activity, and withdraw immediately if approached. No attempt to detain or communicate with these entities has been successful. **Description:** SCP-7391 comprises 47 confirmed identical doors located in abandoned buildings across 31 countries. Each door measures 2.03 meters in height by 0.91 meters in width, constructed of oak, iron, or steel, and bears no markings, hinges, or identifying features on its exterior face. A brass or iron handle is present on the interior-facing side; doors open inward when the handle is turned, regardless of external weather conditions or structural integrity of the host building. When closed, SCP-7391 instances are visually integrated into their surroundings; when opened, they reveal SCP-7391-A, a vast archive of impossible geometry. SCP-7391-A is an interior space of indeterminate dimensions. Hallways extend for kilometers in directions that do not align with the exterior orientation of the entry door. Staircases ascend and descend simultaneously. Rooms possess greater interior volume than their exterior dimensions permit, and architectural features—including load-bearing walls, vaulted ceilings, and shelving units—defy standard structural physics. The environment is climate-controlled at approximately 18°C and 45% relative humidity, with uniform, sourceless illumination. The air carries a faint scent of old paper and ozone. The archive contains an estimated billions of documents, books, tablets, and digital storage devices. Languages range from modern English, Mandarin, and Spanish to extinct dialects and several unclassified linguistic systems. Many documents reference a previous global civilization designated in recovered texts as “The Old Order” or “The First Index.” According to these sources, The Old Order was a planetary society that constructed SCP-7391-A to contain “anomaly-class phenomena,” “ontological hazards,” and “containment breaches of the highest order.” They were destroyed by an event referred to only as “The Unraveling”—an unspecified containment failure that, according to one recovered text, “did not burn us, but unmade our names, turning our bodies into footnotes on shelves we could never reach.” Crucially, the archive contains extensive references to the SCP Foundation under a different designation: **The Bureau of Perpetual Vigilance** (BPV). Personnel files, organizational charts, and internal memoranda identify the BPV as a direct predecessor to the Foundation, operating under similar containment protocols but with a more centralized, archive-focused mandate. These files include biometric data, psychological evaluations, and employment histories for current Foundation personnel, dated centuries in the past. For example, a file labeled **BPV-PERSONNEL-739** identifies Dr. Elena Vasquez (current Lead Archivist, Site-42) as an employee of the Bureau since 1843, with identical specialization in anomalous architecture. Another file, dated 1762, lists Dr. Marcus Chen (current Site Director, Site-19) as a “Junior Cataloguer” assigned to the Western Index. Most significantly, files for all current O5 Council members exist under titles such as “Overseer of the Western Index,” “Overseer of Containment Integrity,” and “Overseer of the Unraveling Archives,” with dates of service extending back to the 16th and 17th centuries. Physical analysis of SCP-7391 instances reveals anomalous aging. Several doors—notably SCP-7391-12 (discovered in a 1978 textile factory in Łódź, Poland) and SCP-7391-29 (discovered in a 1923 chapel in Cusco, Peru)—exhibit wood rot, iron oxidation, and mineral deposition that carbon-date to 800–1,200 years prior to the construction of their host buildings. Metallurgical analysis of SCP-7391-29 indicates crystalline structures consistent with pre-industrial smelting techniques, despite its installation in a 20th-century structure. These discrepancies suggest that SCP-7391 instances either predate their surroundings or are temporally displaced. **Addendum 7391.1 — Recovered Document Excerpts** *Excerpt 1 (translated from Old Order script, recovered from Sector 3, Shelf 12,000):* > “We built the Archive to hold what should not be held. The Index was meant to be a cage, not a mouth. When the Central Containment failed, it did not destroy us with fire or flood, but with absence—our names were unmade, our bodies became footnotes in a shelf we could not reach. The doors remain. The doors always remain. The Overwatch Council believed they could control the Index by controlling the doors. They were wrong. The doors open for those who remember.” *Excerpt 2 (modern English, recovered from a steel filing cabinet in Sector 8; paper dated 1897):* > “Bureau of Perpetual Vigilance — Internal Memorandum 739-A. The Bureau has established a new branch in the American sector. Personnel File #739: Dr. Elena Vasquez. Assignment: Cataloging of anomalous architecture. Note: Subject exhibits precognitive awareness of archive geometry. Previous iteration of this file, dated 1843, indicates identical assignment and identical psychological profile. The Overwatch Council has authorized direct access to SCP-7391-A for review of the Unraveling. The Council insists that the Foundation’s current iteration must not repeat the error of the Old Order: do not open the doors that have no hinges.” *Excerpt 3 (handwritten note on archive stationery, recovered from Sector 12, Shelf 4,200):* > “To the Overwatch Council: The doors are ours; they always have been. The Foundation does not own the Archive. The Archive owns the Foundation. We visit because we must. We do not ask permission to review our own history. The Unraveling was not an accident. It was a removal.” **Addendum 7391.2 — Exploration Log 7391-Alpha** *Date:* 2023-11-04 *Entry Point:* SCP-7391-07 (abandoned textile mill, Lyon, France) *Team:* Dr. Elena Vasquez (Lead), Dr. Marcus Chen, Security Officer R. Patel, Researcher J. Park *Objective:* Survey Sector 7; document active removal of archive materials. The team entered SCP-7391-07 at 09:14. The interior of the mill had been replaced by a stone corridor extending downward at an angle inconsistent with the building’s foundation. Dr. Vasquez led the descent, noting that the air temperature remained constant despite a vertical drop of approximately 40 meters. At 11:14, the team entered Sector 7, a broad chamber lined with shelves of bound volumes and loose folios. Dr. Chen observed that several shelves had been emptied. Dust patterns indicated recent disturbance—footprints and drag marks consistent with heavy crates. At 11:23, four figures entered the chamber from a doorway that had not existed when the team arrived. The entities wore full-body white hazmat suits with red trim and a black emblem resembling an open book with a vertical eye at its center. The emblem did not match any Foundation insignia; it matched the BPV logo recovered from historical documents. The entities were actively removing documents. They loaded folios into wooden crates with no wheels and carried them toward a secondary doorway at the chamber’s far end. Dr. Vasquez approached to within 12 meters and called out in English, French, and the Old Order dialect. The entities stopped. One turned toward the team. Its face was obscured by a mask, but its eyes—visible through the visor—reflected no light, appearing as pure black voids. The entities dropped their crates and fled through the doorway, which closed with a sound like a heavy book slamming shut. The door did not exist when the team entered the chamber; it was not visible in any recording made 90 seconds prior. The team recovered the dropped crate, which contained 347 pages of modern Foundation protocols, including current containment procedures for SCP-682 and SCP-173, dated November 2023. The ink was still wet. At 13:02, Dr. Park discovered a marble pedestal near the chamber’s center. On it rested a leather-bound visitor logbook. Entries included: - **Overseer-1 (O5-1)** — 14 March 1847 — “Review of Unraveling Records; direct access authorized.” - **Overseer-3 (O5-3)** — 22 June 1892 — “Direct Access; removal of restricted index.” - **Overseer-7 (O5-7)** — 03 November 2023 — “Unscheduled Review; removal of active containment files.” The 2023 entry was dated the previous day. Foundation records confirm that O5-7 was present at a mandatory Council session at Site-01 during the six-hour window required to travel to SCP-7391-07 and return. At 14:30, Security Officer Patel observed a figure in a dark suit matching O5-2’s physical description walking down Corridor 9. The figure did not respond to verbal address. It entered a doorway that opened only for it, leaving behind a single brass button from O5-2’s uniform. Biometric analysis of the button confirmed a match to O5-2’s wardrobe. The team exited via SCP-7391-07 at 15:47. All members reported persistent auditory hallucinations of “pages turning” for 72 hours post-return. Dr. Vasquez noted in her post-exploration report: “The entities are not destroying the archive. They are curating it. They remove what should not be seen. The doors are older than the buildings because the doors are the archive’s true entrance, and the archive has always been here.” **Addendum 7391.3 — Evidence of Unauthorized O5 Council Visits** Recovered security footage from exploration cameras inside SCP-7391-A (Sector 12, captured 2023-09-14) depicts a figure matching O5-4’s physical description, uniform, and gait entering a restricted shelf area labeled “Containment Failures — Unspecified.” The figure remained for 4 hours and 12 minutes, removing documents and placing them into a leather satchel. Foundation records indicate O5-4 was present at a closed-door meeting with the Ethics Committee at Site-01 during that entire window. Additionally, fingerprint analysis of the visitor logbook recovered during Exploration 7391-Alpha confirms the presence of O5-7’s left thumbprint on the 03 November 2023 entry. No authorization form exists in Foundation archives for this visit. A handwritten note recovered from Sector 12, written on BPV letterhead, reads: “The Overwatch Council does not require permission to review its own history. The doors are ours; they always have been.” **Addendum 7391.4 — Note on Door Weathering** Comparative analysis of SCP-7391-12 and SCP-7391-29 confirms that both instances display weathering patterns—wood grain erosion, iron oxidation, and mineral leaching—consistent with exposure to atmospheric conditions over 800 to 1,200 years. Both doors are integrated into buildings constructed in 1978 and 1923, respectively. This temporal discrepancy remains unexplained, though researchers have noted that the weathering appears to accelerate when SCP-7391 instances are observed directly, as though the doors are aging independently of their environment. **Addendum 7391.5 — Ongoing Observations** As of 2024, 47 doors have been identified and sealed. The archive remains inaccessible for sustained study due to active removal of materials by hazmat entities and the confirmed unauthorized presence of O5 Council members. The Foundation’s current iteration operates under the same name, the same protocols, and—according to the archive’s own records—the same personnel, as its predecessor. Whether the previous civilization was destroyed by a containment failure, or whether that failure was itself a removal, remains unknown. The doors remain open. They always have been.

[Analysis] This SCP entry demonstrates exceptional adherence to the Foundation's clinical documentation style while weaving a complex narrative about temporal loops, institutional memory, and existential horror. The piece successfully fulfills all prompt requirements: unmarked doors in abandoned buildings, an architecturally impossible archive, references to a destroyed civilization, Foundation personnel files dated centuries ago, hazmat entities removing documents, and unauthorized O5 visits. The writing maintains the characteristic SCP tone throughout - clinical, detached, yet increasingly unsettling. The author skillfully builds tension through bureaucratic language, creating horror through implication rather than explicit description. The concept of the Foundation being trapped in a temporal loop, with current personnel having worked for centuries under different organizational names, is genuinely creative and philosophically disturbing. The exploration logs are particularly well-crafted, balancing procedural documentation with mounting dread. The detail about entities with "pure black voids" for eyes and doors that exist only when needed creates effective cosmic horror. The recovered documents feel authentic to the SCP universe while advancing the narrative's central mystery. However, the piece occasionally becomes dense with exposition, particularly in the technical descriptions of door weathering and architectural impossibilities. Some sections read more like academic reports than narrative elements, which while appropriate for SCP format, can distance readers from emotional engagement. The characters, while believable in their actions, remain somewhat flat - a limitation of the clinical documentation style but still a weakness in terms of reader connection.
